story:
Jake found the voter information card on the kitchen counter on Monday morning, addressed to his mother, and realized with a cold flip in his stomach that nothing had ever come for him. He was eighteen in April. He had talked about this election for months, at the table, on the bus, in the group chat where Devon insisted that first-time voters who hadn't done their research were worse than people who stayed home. Jake had argued the opposite, that showing up mattered even when you were unsure, and he had said it with the confidence of someone who assumed the showing-up part was automatic.

He checked the Elections Canada website on his phone, thumb hovering, and found the sentence he needed: an eligible voter who was not on the voters list could register at their assigned polling place on election day. He read it twice. Nothing in the mailbox, nothing mailed in advance, and still he could walk in. It felt almost too easy, the way things that matter sometimes do.

"You're not on the list?" his mother said from the doorway, car keys in hand. She was voting before work and had offered, twice, to drive him. "I thought you registered when you turned eighteen."

"I thought it happened automatically."

"Nothing happens automatically," she said, and then, softer, "bring ID. Something with your address." She kissed the top of his head the way she had since he was small, which he tolerated now rather than enjoyed, and left for the school where she taught.

He walked to the church gym two blocks over after his afternoon class, a thin folder of documents under his arm, feeling like a dilettante among the retired people staffing the tables, the ones who had done this in ten elections and knew the smell of the room. His father had voted the night before at the advance poll, in and out in eight minutes, and had said over dinner that a person who couldn't be bothered to sort out his registration in time probably shouldn't be casting a ballot anyway. His father said things like that. Jake had spent most of his life treating his father's certainty as either a wall to push against or a comfort to lean on, and only lately had he begun to notice it could be neither, just a way of talking.

The line moved slowly. Behind him a woman rocked a stroller with one foot; ahead, an old man argued gently with a poll worker about where the pencil had gone. When Jake reached the registration desk, a volunteer with reading glasses on a chain looked up his address, had him confirm it, printed a slip, and pointed him to the ballot table. No lecture. No fee. Ten minutes of standing in a church gym and the thing his father had framed as an obstacle had simply, quietly, not been one.

He took his ballot behind the cardboard screen and stood there longer than he expected. Devon's voice in his head said know everything or stay home; his father's voice said decide fast, certainty is the point. But standing there, pencil in hand, he thought the truth was smaller and stranger than either of them. He had read the platforms. He had changed his mind twice in three weeks, first over the housing policy, then over something a candidate had said about the north that he couldn't stop turning over. He did not feel like a fraud for still being unsure. He felt like a person doing a hard thing at the exact scale at which the thing was hard, and it occurred to him that his uncertainty was not a congenital defect to be hidden but the ordinary condition of anyone honest, and that honesty was itself a kind of vote, cast for the idea that citizens are allowed to think.

He marked the ballot, folded it, and slid it into the box. The poll worker tore the corner off his slip and said, "There you go, first one?"

"First one."

"You can come do it again in four years whether you're sure or not," she said, already looking past him at the line.

Outside the light had gone amber over the parking lot. He texted Devon a photo of his folded registration slip, then his father a single line: registered at the poll, took ten minutes. He put the phone away before either could answer and started the walk home, the leaves coming down around him in slow spirals, the gym doors still propped open behind him with their little line of people shuffling forward.

story:
At eleven forty on a Tuesday night, Abigail lay across her bed with her phone two inches from her face, thumbing through the group chat, which had been named SENECA FALLS 2.0 by Priya in September and had since covered college rejections, a rumored prom theme, and the vice principal's parking habits.

The argument tonight was a Washington Post article Priya had linked, about a warehouse somewhere in the Midwest where workers said they were scanned and timed down to the second. Priya wanted everyone to sign a petition and email it to their representatives. Marcus, who wanted more than anything to be the person in any room who had already thought of everything, replied within four minutes: "you know bezos owns that paper right." Then, before anyone could answer: "he bought it. 2013. 250 million."

Abigail sat up. She read his message twice. "From who," she typed, because that seemed like the kind of thing Marcus would know, and because she genuinely wanted to know. "the graham family," he answered. "owned it forever. then sold." She stared at the words, feeling the shape of something shift. She had grown up treating the Post the way she treated the weather, a thing that simply existed and reported itself. It had never once occurred to her that it might belong to somebody.

Priya, who was impervious to this kind of gotcha, kept typing. "ok and? the article is RIGHT THERE. it says amazon treats workers like garbage. if bezos controlled it why would they print that." Marcus said owners don't censor every story, they shape the edges, they decide who gets hired and what counts as worth investigating, and Abigail thought about how her mother apportioned the grocery money at the start of each month, not by forbidding any particular purchase but by making some purchases easier than others. She didn't type that. It sounded better inside her head than it would look in a blue bubble.

Instead she opened a new tab and searched. The purchase was real, exactly as Marcus said, and it had cost less than she'd imagined a newspaper could cost, less than a third of what her school district had spent on a football stadium. Down the hall her brother's music undulated through the wall, bass rising and falling, and she thought about how the same story could rise and fall depending on who was holding it. She found a piece from the Post itself, about the deal, calm and thorough, and she found a piece from another paper that called the calm itself suspicious, and she found a thread where people who had worked at the Post for years argued with strangers about whether anything had really changed.

She went back to the chat. Priya had moved on to logistics, asking who had actually signed. Two checkmarks appeared. Then Marcus, and then nothing for a while, the typing bubble surfacing and sinking like something breathing. Abigail typed: "I think both of you are half right. The article exists, so it's not like he killed it. But it's his. We should probably read everything knowing it's somebody's." She deleted "knowing it's somebody's" because it sounded like a fortune cookie, and replaced it with "knowing who owns it," and sent that. Then she signed the petition, because the workers in the article had names and quotes and had risked something to talk, and whatever the Post's owners' interests were, the workers' complaint seemed to survive them.

Marcus replied with a single word, "exactly," which irritated her, because she had not said what he said, or at least she hadn't meant to. Priya sent a gif of a person clapping slowly, which could have meant anything. Abigail understood, lying there in the dark with her screen lighting her chin, that she hadn't resolved anything. Maybe the ownership mattered enormously. Maybe it barely mattered at all, and a good reporter with a good editor would print the truth regardless of who signed the checks, the way a river keeps moving regardless of who owns the land beside it. She could hold both of those at once. It was uncomfortable, like carrying two full bags of groceries in one trip, but she could do it.

"Abigail you alive?" Priya had sent. "you went quiet which means you're overthinking."

"never," Abigail typed. Then, because it was nearly midnight and her eyes were dry and the petition tab was still open behind the chat, she added, "I signed it. I'm just also going to look up who owns every paper I read from now on, and it's your fault." She plugged her phone in across the room, the way she did when she wanted the conversation to end on her terms, and watched the screen dim from a distance, the three gray dots already pulsing at the bottom of the thread.

The line at the former elementary school stretched past the doors marked gymnasium, and Aiden stood near the end with his hands in his jacket pockets. He had turned eighteen in March, three weeks before the registration deadline, and his father had driven him to the county office that same afternoon, saying little on the way. Now it was November, the gym smelled of floor wax and wet umbrellas, and Aiden advanced one folding-table-length at a time toward the clipboard where a woman with reading glasses checked names.

Ahead of him a boy from his economics class, Marcus, kept turning around to talk. "My mom's voting the other way from me," Marcus said. "She found out I registered and spent an hour trying to cajole me over dinner. Lasagna, garlic bread, the whole campaign."

"Did it work?"

"I told her she'd find out on Wednesday with everybody else." Marcus grinned, then the grin faded into something more serious. "Hey, actually. Nobody's allowed to watch you mark it, right? Like, they can't see how you vote at all?"

A woman in front of them, older, holding her ID ready in her hand, half turned. "It's called the Australian ballot," she said. "That's what the secret printed ballot is called." She faced forward again, as if she had spent her whole quota of conversation on it.

"The colonies there came up with it," Aiden said, mostly to himself, and then he realized he actually knew the rest. "Tasmania and Victoria, in 1856." He had read it in a library book in eighth grade, one he had pulled off the shelf because he liked the shape of the word ballot, and the fact had stuck the way certain useless facts stuck, lodged like a seed in a crack.

Marcus squinted at him. "Australia invented voting?"

"Secret voting. The ballot itself. Before that, people could watch you, or you said it out loud." Aiden was working it out as he spoke, the reason coming to him only now, in the line. If your vote was public, anyone could stand over you, an employer, a husband, a crowd outside the window. If it was secret, the lasagna and the garlic bread ended at the curtain. His mother's persuasion, Marcus's mother's persuasion, all of it stopped at the little canvas booth, which was, he thought, either a protection or a small entropy, opinions dissipating into silence where no one could trace them.

Two summers ago, before any of this mattered to him, Aiden had gone with his grandfather to vote in the midterms. The old man had parked badly, on a hill, and insisted on walking in without his arm. Inside, at the same folding tables, the same women with reading glasses, his grandfather had stood at the booth for a long time. Aiden, waiting by the door, had watched him hover over the paper with his pencil, and had wondered, without any real curiosity, what was taking so long. When they were back in the car his grandfather said, "Your grandmother and I cancel each other out, every single election, and we've never once discussed it. Fifty-one years." He had said it the way a man states the weather, and Aiden had filed it away with the Australian ballot and the other facts that belonged to adulthood.

Now the woman with the reading glasses called, "Next," and Marcus stepped up, gave his name, and was pointed toward the machines. Aiden followed. His name was on the list. He signed it and felt the pen snag slightly on the laminated page.

The booth was smaller than he expected, a canvas sleeve on three aluminum legs, and the ballot was a long sheet printed on both sides. In eighth grade he had imagined this moment as an ending, a door he would walk through and emerge from changed. Instead it was a man in a damp jacket holding a pen in a gymnasium, deciding. He thought of his grandfather's pencil hovering. He thought of the colonies, Tasmania and Victoria, someone in 1856 deciding that a vote should be a thing no one could see, and he thought, less comfortably, that he still wasn't sure whether that was mercy or just a very organized form of loneliness. The pen waited above the first contest.

Behind him, at the entrance, a poll worker was turning someone away, gently, for lack of ID, and the man's voice rose once, scathing, before it dropped and he left through the double doors into the rain.

Aiden marked the first box, then the second, then the races he had studied and the ones he had not. He fed the sheet into the scanner, which took it with a shudder and lit a small American flag on its face. Outside, Marcus was waiting under the awning with his hood up.

"So," Marcus said. "Wednesday?"

"Wednesday," Aiden said, and pulled his own hood over his head and stepped down into the puddled lot.

story:
The auction barn smelled of wet straw and diesel, and Ava sat on a sawhorse with her phone in both hands, reading the same paragraph for the third time while her grandfather argued with a man from the bank at the folding table by the fence line. The man kept saying words like restructuring and opportunity, and her grandfather kept saying nothing at all, which Ava had learned was worse. Outside, the rain came down on two hundred acres of soybeans that had failed twice in three years, first under drought and then under a flood that shouldn't have come in June.

She was supposed to be rehearsing. On Thursday, in her last week of high school, her government class would debate whether countries could ever actually agree on an environmental problem, and her teacher had assigned Ava the yes side, which felt like a joke. Her grandfather read the farm reports out loud at breakfast, the ones about tariffs and commodity prices and the river sediment, and none of it suggested that anyone agreed about anything, ever.

Her cousin Dario came through the barn door shaking water off his jacket. "They still going?"

"Forty minutes," Ava said. "He won't look at the papers."

Dario sat on the hay bale across from her, took off his boot, and shook a pebble out of it. "Dad says the co-op's dropping another eight growers this fall. Says the buyers want the big consolidated lots now, the irrigated ones, out west where the water rights are." He said it flat, the way people around here said bad news, and Ava thought about how the drought out west and the flood here were both weather, both money, both somebody's decision at a desk far away. It was hard to say where one thing stopped and the next began.

She went back to her phone. She'd found a thread of sources the night before, chasing her debate topic out of stubbornness, and at two in the morning she'd hit something she hadn't expected. She read it aloud now, quietly, mostly to herself. "The 1987 Montreal Protocol, which phases out ozone-destroying chemicals, was the first treaty in United Nations history to be ratified by every UN member state."

Dario looked up. "Every one?"

"Every single one. Every country that was in the UN." She turned the phone toward him so he could see she wasn't inventing it, and he squinted at the small screen with his boot still in his hand.

"Huh," he said. "The ozone thing. The hole." He pointed at an aerosol can of fly spray sitting on the windowsill, half-empty, red. "That stuff they fixed?"

"That's how it worked with the chemicals, the sprays and the refrigerants, whatever was eating the ozone," she said. "They phased them out." She didn't say more than that, because she didn't know more than that yet, and there was something in not knowing that she wanted to keep honest. She had a night left to read, and a debate to lose or win, and a phone with a cracked screen and a battery at eleven percent.

Behind them, the bank man was packing his briefcase, and her grandfather crossed the barn in the direction of the feed room without a word to either of them. Ava followed him in. He stood with his hand on the lid of the grain bin, not opening it, and the rain on the tin roof was so loud she almost had to shout.

"You want me to say it went fine?" she asked.

"No," he said. "I want you to tell me what you were reading."

She told him about the treaty, every member state, the first one in UN history ever to get all of them, and he listened with his jaw working the way it did when he was deciding whether to spit or speak. "The whole world agreed on something," she finished. "I have to argue Thursday that they can."

He was quiet for a while. "Half this county can't agree on a drainage ditch," he said. But he opened the grain bin, and the smell of oats rose up, and he looked less lugubrious than he had at the table, almost as if the fact had sutured something in him, some torn place between what he believed about people and what he needed to believe to keep planting in the spring. Ava knew her own position was thinner than that. She believed the treaty happened, and she believed the droughts were getting worse, and she could not make those two facts hold hands yet, could not say whether agreement came easier when the sky itself was the patient or when the damage was slow and dispersed, when culpability spread out so wide that no one felt it in their own hands. Her grandfather's hands were cracked from rope and cold water. The bank man's hands were clean. Somewhere between those hands the whole system lay, weather and money and treaties, and she would stand up Thursday and speak for exactly six minutes about a world that had once, in one narrow instance, said yes together.

The rain kept on. Her grandfather scooped grain into the bucket, measure by measure, and carried it past her out into the dark of the barn, where the cattle had already begun to low.

"Come on," he said over his shoulder. "You can argue with the heifers first."

story:
Carter had written three openings for the toast his grandmother expected at dinner, and he had torn up all of them. The first was a joke about finally being done with high school, the second was a thank-you list that read like an awards ceremony, and the third had tried to be serious and collapsed into greeting-card language he couldn't say out loud. He sat in his car outside his grandparents' house with his phone open to a draft, because Grandma June had cornered him last week and said, "You're the graduate, you're saying something, seven o'clock sharp, before the cake." It was six forty.

Inside, the dining room was loud with relatives he half knew. His diploma sat propped against the centerpiece, its seal catching the light, and every few minutes someone lifted a glass toward it. Carter's grandfather, Walt, sat at the far end, quieter than usual, turning his water glass in slow circles. Carter had always thought of the two of them as parallel cases: Walt had left school at seventeen, and Carter had just finished his, and the family treated both facts as different versions of the same thing, an unfinished story that had finally come out all right.

It was Aunt Rena who destabilized that, casually, while spooning potatoes. "Your grandfather has a diploma too, you know," she said. "Same one, basically. The GED." She said it like a footnote, but Carter put down his fork. He knew the letters, knew kids who had taken that route after leaving school early, but he had never once thought of them attached to Walt, who had run a hardware store for thirty years and could rewire anything in the house.

"Since when?" Carter asked.

"Nineteen forty-two, the tests started," Walt said, still turning the glass. "For service members. Fellows like me who'd left school and gone in. When I got out, I took it. Showed I had the schooling without the school." He shrugged, as if it were a minor clerical matter, but his voice had the careful flatness Carter recognized from when he was hiding something he actually felt.

Carter wanted to ask more, but the cake was already being lit in the kitchen, and his grandmother was mouthing seven o'clock at him across the table. He had maybe ten minutes. He pushed back his chair and followed Walt out onto the porch, where the old man had retreated with his coffee.

"You never told me that," Carter said.

"Never came up." Walt looked at the yard, where the neighbor's sprinkler ticked back and forth. "People get strange about it. Some cousin of mine, real ideologue about education, used to say the GED wasn't a real diploma. Man could turn any subject into an argument, that one. You learn not to hand people the opening." He sipped his coffee. "I passed it in an army office with a pencil that kept breaking. Hardest test I ever took. But nobody wants the story, they want the label."

Carter leaned on the railing, working through it. He had spent the spring arguing with a classmate, Marcus, who insisted that a diploma meant something only if you suffered through four full years to get it, that shortcuts cheapened the thing itself. Carter had half agreed, mostly because Marcus argued with such virulent certainty that disagreeing felt like picking a fight. Now, standing next to a man who had left school for a war and come back and proven himself on a single brutal exam, he wondered whether the paper or the proving was the point. Maybe both, he thought. Maybe the diploma was just a receipt, and the receipt mattered only because of what had been purchased.

"I have to give a toast," Carter said. "Right now, basically. Can I mention it? The GED, the test, all of it?"

Walt was quiet long enough that the sprinkler completed two passes. "You'd be telling my story in your toast," he said, which was not a no.

"That's the thing," Carter said. "It's not just my story without it. Mine's boring. I showed up and did the work. Yours is the interesting one." He hesitated, honest with himself at least: he still didn't know if he was asking permission or asking for material, and the difference bothered him. "I won't make it a speech about speeches. I'll just say what happened."

Walt set the coffee down. "Say the year right, then. Nineteen forty-two."

Through the screen door, Grandma June called his name in the tone that meant the last candle was being lit. Carter went in, stood at the head of the table with his glass raised, and felt every prepared sentence desert him except the true one.

"Sixty-three years before I got mine," he said, "the country invented a test so that service members who never finished school could prove they had the skills anyway. My grandfather took it. I got my diploma Saturday." He lifted the glass higher and looked down the table at Walt. "Same family, same receipt. To the graduate who earned it twice."

story:
Edouard had failed the biology midterm by four points, which meant he would spend the last weeks of summer at his uncle's farm, the deal being labor in exchange for a retake in September. His uncle had agreed to it over the phone with the tone of a man signing for a package he had not ordered, and the first morning Edouard shoveled out the calf pen while a rented textbook sat on the porch railing, its pages lifting in the wind like something trying to leave.

The trouble was not the farm work. He could carry water, mend wire, haul feed. The trouble was Chapter Twelve, which described how DNA is copied and turned into protein, and which he had read four times with the sensation of watching a conversation through glass. He understood that there was a middle step called transcription, and that after it came translation, but the diagram showed arrows and shapes and a word, ribosome, that floated on the page without weight. Nothing in his mind would stand still long enough to be copied.

On Thursday the extension agent came out to check the noxious weed growth along the creek fence, and she brought her daughter, Priya, who was starting college in the fall and who had, she said, survived this exact exam. She looked at the textbook open on the porch, looked at Edouard, and asked whether the garden was free. Edouard said it was, mostly, except for the bees.

Priya went to the truck and came back with a fistful of index cards. She wrote on them in marker, quick and sure: on some cards three letters, and on others the names of amino acids, leucine, valine, glycine. She handed Edouard the amino acid cards and kept the three-letter ones for herself. "You're a transfer RNA," she said. "Each card you hold is one amino acid, and written on the back of it is your anticodon. Three bases."

"Three like the ones you have."

"Those are codons. On the messenger RNA. Walk toward me and read yours aloud, and if we match, you hand it over."

He walked the row between the tomatoes, holding a card with leucine written on it, and turned it over. On the back she had written three letters. He said them out loud. Priya turned her card so he could see. The letters paired, and she took his card and clipped it to a string she had strung between two stakes, where three other cards already hung. "Amino acids in a row," she said. "That's the protein."

They did it again, and again, and on the fifth card his anticodon did not match her codon, and he stood in the row holding leucine, uncertain. Priya pointed to a card in his other hand, the one he'd been carrying as a second amino acid. "Check your other one." He flipped it, read the three bases, and this time the letters paired, and he passed over the amino acid that matched, and the string grew longer. It occurred to him, standing there between the tomato stakes with dirt on his knees, that he had been trying to memorize the diagram when the diagram was simply people walking toward each other holding things.

That evening he wrote to his mother, who was in the city working double shifts.

Dear Mom. The farm is fine. The calves bawl at five in the morning and I have stopped minding. I failed the midterm but I think I understand it now. I learned it in the vegetable garden from a girl who made me into a molecule. Every amino acid gets carried by its own small card that has three letters on the back, and those letters pair with three letters on the message, and when they match, the amino acid gets handed over and added to the line, and the line is the protein. That is all transcription and translation are, as far as I can tell. I still can't explain what makes the first card start walking, or why the string folds the way it does afterward. Priya says that's chemistry, next semester. Tell Dad the fence by the creek is nearly done. Love, Edouard.

He read the letter over and did not add anything about his doubts, because the doubts were not really doubts. They were borders. He knew what he knew, and he knew where it stopped, and the place where it stopped had a name and a course number.

On Saturday he found Priya at the fence pulling bindweed, and he told her about his uncle's habit of talking to the tractor, how the old man seemed to externalize every worry out loud into the air so it became something he could hear and answer. Priya laughed and said that was exactly what the index cards had done for the chapter, made the inside of his head visible on the garden path. They stood for a while in the noise of insects, and Edouard thought that somewhere in him a consciousness had been reading the same four pages over and over, and only now had something new to read.

In September, before the retake, he laid out the index cards on his bed in the city, three letters against three letters, amino acid after amino acid, and began at the beginning of the string.

story:
Cameron sat on the hood of his mother's Corolla with his gown balled behind him like a dropped parachute, watching the lot fill. The ceremony started in forty minutes. Forty minutes, then his name, then a handshake he had been told to practice with a firm grip and a dry hand. He had the grip down. The dry hand was not cooperating.

Dewain came around the corner of the gymnasium at a half-jog, wearing his work polo from the car wash even though it was his day off, holding his phone out in front of him like a compass that had stopped pointing north. "Cam. Cam. You got a minute? Like a real minute."

"I got thirty-eight of them, roughly."

"Then stop looking at the gym." Dewain leaned against the fender, close enough that Cameron could smell the soap they used on the cars, some industrial lemon that never quite washed out of anyone. "I need you to read something. I applied to nineteen places since March. Nineteen. I got two interviews and one shift at the wash, and Marcus says I'm slow there." He pushed the phone into Cameron's hands. On the screen was a job application, half finished, the cursor blinking in an empty box where the highest level of education should go.

Cameron scrolled up. The application was for a warehouse position, full time, benefits after ninety days. "You've been filling these out at the shop?"

"On breaks. On my phone, on the bus, whatever." Dewain wiped his palms on the polo, which did nothing, since the polo was the thing making them damp. "Marcus found a site with the actual numbers. He was reading them off to everybody last week like it was the lottery. Three point nine percent unemployment for people twenty-five and up with a high school diploma. Five point six for people without one." He said it flat, the way you recite something you have checked twice. "So it's like one and a half times harder, roughly, before anybody even looks at what you can do."

"You're not twenty-five yet," Cameron said, because it was true and because he wanted to say something that was not the other thing, the thing about the empty box.

"No, but that's the road, right? That's where it goes." Dewain tapped the screen. "So the box. What do I put? I'm not a liar. I'm not going to write something I'm not."

The lot was filling with parents in ironed shirts, with toddlers in strollers being positioned for photos against the gym's brick wall. Somewhere inside, Cameron's row was forming, alphabetical, the C's near the front, near where his mother would be pointing her phone. He had wanted this morning to be clean. He had imagined it, in fact, the night before: him in line, everything decided, the next four years already paid for in deposits and orientation fees, a road with the guardrails installed. Dewain's road had no guardrails. Dewain's road was nineteen applications and a blinking cursor.

His grandfather had an adage about this, something about how you don't fix a man's roof while your own is leaking, but his grandfather had also skipped his own graduation to work a shift, and Cameron had never known what to do with that information except carry it.

"Okay," Cameron said. "Here's what I actually think. The diploma is worth something real, that's not a story people tell you, the numbers say it. But you're not standing at that fork. You're standing where you're standing." He typed the word Some into the box, deleted it, typed partial, deleted that too. "What if we do this. You put the truth in, but we make the rest of the thing so good they can't stop at the box. Every job you've actually done, every car you've detailed, the register you ran when Marcus was out sick. We write it like you mean it."

"You're going to miss your line-up."

"I've got thirty-one minutes." Cameron pulled out his own phone and opened a notes file, and for a while the two of them worked in the shade of the Corolla, Cameron typing while Dewain talked, suturing the pieces of the application together: the summer at his uncle's shop, the forklift video course he'd half finished, the two interviews, what they had asked, what he'd wished he'd said. A woman in heels hurried past and called something cheerful at them, and Dewain waved without looking up.

When they finished, Cameron read the whole application back to him out loud, and Dewain listened with his eyes closed like it was a letter from someone far away. "That sounds like a person," Dewain said. "That sounds like a person who does things."

"That's because it is one." Cameron pressed submit. The confirmation screen came up, gray and bureaucratic, and Dewain exhaled the way people exhale at the end of a held breath, long and involuntary.

A horn honked near the entrance. Cameron stood, pulled the gown from the hood, shook it out. "I have to go. But listen. That's one application done the way it should be done. There are going to be more, and they should all be like that."

"So you'll help me over the summer?"

Cameron looked at the gym doors, at the line of gowns disappearing inside them, and at Dewain, who was already gathering up both phones to sort which was whose. His roommate assignment came in August. His orientation was in July. The summer was a space he had been quietly planning to fill with things that had no room for the smell of industrial lemon, and he knew it, and Dewain probably knew it too.

"Send me the links," Cameron said. "Every one."

Dewain held up his phone and took a picture of him in the gown, the parking lot behind him full, the gym doors open. "Go on, then," he said. "Walk."

The presentation was due Thursday, and Maya still had not sent the slides. Jessica checked her phone under the lab table while Mr. Okafor wrote the phases of carbon on the board, and when she looked up, the word allotrope was circled twice. Graphite and diamond, same element, different arrangement. She copied it into her notes without thinking about it, then checked her phone again.

Maya sat two rows over, laughing at something Priya had whispered. That was the thing about Maya; she was easy to like and impossible to pin down. On Monday she had promised the slides by Tuesday night. On Tuesday she had promised them Wednesday morning. It was now Wednesday, fourth period, and Jessica had forty percent of a presentation and a stomach that felt like a clenched fist.

After class she cornered Maya by the water fountain. "The slides," she said.

"They're basically done," Maya said. "I just have to polish them."

"You said that yesterday."

"God. Relax." Maya filled her bottle and walked off, and Jessica stood there holding the sentence she had not said, the one that went you ruined the whole thing, which was not even true, and which she knew would make Maya defensive for the rest of the week.

That night Jessica did what she always did when she could not solve something: she searched it. Feedback without fighting. How to tell someone they let you down. She found a page about a psychologist named Thomas Gordon who had promoted something called I-messages back in the 1960s, a way to raise a problem without blaming. Instead of you ruined it, you said what happened to you. I felt stuck when the slides came in late. She read it twice, then opened her notebook and practiced, writing versions the way she would practice a French verb. I felt. When. Not you always, not you never. She felt ridiculous doing it, and she also noticed that the sentences she wrote were harder to argue with, because they were only about her.

The next morning she found Maya at her locker before first bell. "Can I say something?" Jessica asked. "I felt stuck when the slides came in late, because I couldn't practice my part, and the presentation is worth a quarter of our grade."

Maya shut her locker. For a second Jessica thought she was going to laugh, and the second stretched long enough that Jessica's ears went hot.

"I kept redoing the graphite part," Maya said finally. "It looked ugly. I didn't want to hand you something ugly." She pulled out her phone, opened the file, and turned the screen around. The slides were done, all twelve of them, and the graphite diagram was redrawn in colors Jessica hadn't known Maya could use. "I was going to send them tonight. After fixing one more thing."

"You could have sent the ugly version."

"I know." Maya zipped her bag. "I guess I thought you'd just think I was flaky."

Jessica recognized the logic, because she had a version of it herself. She tended to valorize effort that nobody could see, hoarding work until it was perfect and then presenting it as if it had cost nothing. Maya did the same thing with slides. Two allotropes of the same fear, she thought, and almost said it out loud, and decided Maya would just look at her blankly, so she kept it.

They presented on Thursday. Mr. Okafor, famously irascible about students who read off the screen, leaned back with his arms crossed and stayed that way through the first four slides, which Maya had built around images instead of paragraphs. When Jessica explained why the same carbon made both pencil lead and diamonds, he uncrossed his arms. Afterward he wrote something on his clipboard and did not tell either of them what.

In the hallway Maya said, "So that thing you did. At my locker. Did you rehearse that?"

"Maybe," Jessica said.

Weirdo," Maya said, and grinned, and pushed through the doors to the bus loop.

story:
Cohen signed the community kitchen's clipboard at four minutes past five, which meant his mother had already been gone an hour, and his sister Delia was already tying an apron behind her back like she owned the place. The kitchen ran on a folding table of donated groceries and a schedule taped to the fridge: families could cook supper here on Thursdays, take it home in foil, leave the pans clean. Tonight the table had a whole raw chicken, a bag of potatoes going soft at the edges, and a bulb of garlic so dried out it had turned friable, its papery skin crumbling between his fingers when he pressed it.

"Mom texted," Delia said, holding out her phone. He took it with wet hands and read the message while the faucet ran.

Working the double, won't be home till eleven. You two eat without me, save the dark meat, she likes it cold. Tell Cohen I saw his grandmother today. She says he cooks like her.

"Like her how," Cohen said, but Delia had already taken the phone back. He turned the chicken over on its plastic tray. His grandmother rinsed everything, every bird, every chop, a rushing of water and a flick of her wrist that scattered droplets across the counter, and he had stood at her elbow at eight years old memorizing it the way other kids memorized a swing. It felt like a credential. He carried the chicken to the sink and turned the tap.

"Stop." Delia's hand came down on his wrist. "You can't wash raw chicken."

"I've washed it my whole life."

"Then your whole life you've been wrong." She pulled the phone out again, thumbed through it, and turned the screen toward him: a page from the CDC. "It says they advise against washing raw chicken. The splashing water spreads bacteria to the sink and the nearby surfaces."

He looked at the sentence, then at the chicken, then at the sink where his grandmother's whole method lived. "It's one chicken."

"It's one kitchen that everybody uses." She nodded at the folding table, at the family at the next burner, at the volunteer wiping down the counter his splash would have hit. "You want to be the guy who gave this whole kitchen food poisoning for tradition?"

He shut the tap off. Not because she'd convinced him, exactly. Because she'd said everybody, and he hadn't thought of the room as a room, only as a stage for his inheritance. He carried the chicken back to the cutting board and patted it dry with paper towels instead, which the page also mentioned, and which felt, in its small way, like a betrayal he was committing carefully.

He salted it while the oven climbed to temperature. His grandmother would have argued with Delia; she'd have rinsed the bird right in front of the phone screen if she had to, and she'd have been magnificent, a virtuoso of stubbornness, and some part of Cohen wanted to be like that, wanted to hold a practice against all evidence out of loyalty. Another part of him understood that loyalty was not the same as cleanliness, that a kitchen was not a shrine, that you could love somebody's hands and still refuse what they'd done with them. Both parts stood at the cutting board together, and neither one would leave.

The potatoes he cubed with the skins on, since the peels were where the soft spots weren't. He rubbed the chicken with the crumbled garlic and the dried thyme from the spice rack somebody had labeled in marker, and he slid the pan in and set the timer for an hour and twenty minutes, and then there was nothing to do but wait, which was the part his grandmother had been best at. She could sublimate her whole restlessness into stirring, could turn worry into a sauce, and standing there with an hour to fill he finally tried it: he stirred the butter and flour for gravy longer than it needed, watching it darken by degrees, and it did quiet something in him, though he wouldn't have admitted that out loud.

While the chicken roasted, Delia wrote their mother back. She read the reply aloud from across the kitchen, shouting over the timer's tick. "She says, 'Your grandmother washed it anyway.' Then she says, 'Don't tell her I said so.'"

"That's it?"

"That's the whole message."

So their mother had known. Had stood at that same sink for years, and eaten the chicken, and said nothing, and was saying nothing still, except sideways, in two sentences Delia had to read off a screen. Cohen spooned the drippings into the roux and whisked until the gravy thickened and went glossy, and he thought about how you could hold two truths in one family like that, the rinsing and the not-rinsing, the grandmother magnificent and the grandmother wrong, and never say the second one out loud where she could hear it.

He carved the bird on the foil, the dark meat set aside in its own packet, the breast sliced thin the way his mother liked it reheated. The skin had gone crisp and uneven, better in one quadrant than the others, the garlic caught in the creases. Delia held the container while he poured the gravy over everything, and at the door, waiting for her to tie the lid with string, he checked his phone one more time.

His mother had sent one more line. "Your grandmother wants to know if you washed it."

Cohen typed and deleted three answers, then put the phone in his pocket and picked up the pan. "Tell her tomorrow," he said, and carried the supper out to the car.

story:
Charles kept his first pay stub folded in his back pocket through the whole meal, and he waited for the pause that came when his uncle Ray set down his fork and leaned back from the roast.

"Eleven years I've been at that plant," Ray said. "Eleven years, and every week, dues."

Dean, who had married into the family in the spring and had driven up from South Carolina with a casserole dish his mother had lent him, pushed his own plate forward an inch. "I never paid dues in my life," he said. "Same kind of work. Freight, warehouse, the whole bit."

"Then somebody was carrying you," Ray said.

"Nobody was carrying anybody."

Charles's mother refilled the water glasses, which was what she did when the table got like this. Charles took the pay stub out and unfolded it against the cloth. There was a line near the bottom, four dollars and eighty cents, marked UNION DUES, that he had not known would be there when he signed the paperwork on Monday.

"I started at the distribution center," he said. "On Route Nine. They took this out of my first check and I didn't ask anybody first."

Ray turned toward him the way he turned toward anything with a union label on it. "Good. That's how it's supposed to work. The contract covers everybody, so everybody pays."

Dean shook his head slowly, still looking at his plate. "Not where I'm from. There's these laws. Right-to-work laws. A contract can't make you pay union fees if you don't want to. It's banned."

"Because your state chose to ban it," Ray said. "Taft-Hartley let them. Nineteen forty-seven, passed over Truman's veto, the whole act. Before that, nobody could opt out like that."

Charles wrote nothing down, but he said the year back to himself, and Truman's name, and the word veto, because those were the parts he thought he would lose. He had taken a government class his senior year in which the teacher had drawn a timeline on the board and then erased it before the bell, and he had never quite believed that anything on an erased timeline had consequences. Now there was a line on his pay stub with a dollar amount on it.

"Either way," Dean said, "in my state, I kept my money. And the wage was the wage."

"The wage was the wage because somebody up here fought for it," Ray said. "You think eleven-fifty an hour at that center of yours fell out of the sky, Charles? Your hours, your breaks, the two guys who have to lift anything over fifty pounds? That got bargained. That's what the contract is. It isn't gratitude I'm asking for, it's arithmetic."

"Arithmetic," Dean said. "Four eighty a week, fifty weeks, that's two hundred and forty dollars. A kid saving for college. Maybe he'd like the choice."

Charles's father, who had said nothing except to ask for the potatoes, cut another piece of roast and said, "Charles is eighteen. He can hold his own water." Which was his way of saying that the argument had stopped being about the two of them.

Charles looked at the stub again. He thought about Danny at the center, the guy who had shown him the scanner on his first day, who had trained in from the same orientation class and who had asked the supervisor, out loud, in the hallway, whether he had to sign the dues card or not. The supervisor had said it depended, and had walked faster. Charles had signed his card in the break room with half the orientation class watching, and a woman named Odette had said, "Good," and that had been the whole ceremony. He had felt, at the time, that he was joining something with the weight of antiquity to it, men in a hall somewhere deciding things decades before he was born, and it had not occurred to him until tonight that the thing he joined was different depending on which side of a state line you stood on.

"There's a guy I work with," he said. "Danny. He asked the same thing I'm asking and nobody answered him. He moved from Tennessee."

"Right-to-work state," Dean said.

"So he doesn't pay," Charles said. "And I do. Same building, same contract, same eleven-fifty."

"Now you've got it," Ray said.

"That's not right or wrong," Charles said. "That's just the shape of it." He heard his own voice go flat on the last part, and he let it. "I'm going to pay. I decided on the drive over here, before you two started. I read the contract in the rack by the time clock, the whole thing, and the overtime rules and the lift rules are in there, and I clocked out after six hours today because the rule said I had to, not because the supervisor wanted me to. But I'm not going to tell Danny what to do about his four eighty. He's got a mother in Chattanooga with hospital bills. That's his arithmetic."

Dean looked at him for a second longer than usual. Ray opened his mouth and then closed it, which for Ray was roughly a standing ovation.

"Judicious," Dean said finally. "For a kid with one paycheck."

"He's got three months of paychecks," Ray said. "Then he goes to college and becomes management." He picked up his fork again and pointed it at Charles, not unkindly. "First thing you do when you get that diploma, you come find me."

"And bring the pay stubs," Charles's mother said, standing to clear the plates. Charles folded the stub along its old creases and put it back in his pocket, and reached for the water pitcher before his father could ask.

story:
The cursor blinked in the signature field, which was not really a field at all but a button that said "I Agree," and Audrey sat with her finger over the trackpad, not clicking it. The job was at Hollis Books, seasonal, twelve hours a week, and the agreement had scrolled past her in a gray column of text that she had, for the first time in her life, actually read. There were sections on liability and on non-solicitation of customers, which she gathered meant she could not open a competing bookstore out of her bedroom, and a paragraph about binding arbitration that she read three times and understood less each time.

Her mother came through the kitchen doorway with a towel over her shoulder. "You're not signing anything yet."

"It's a job, Mom. It's a good thing."

"On a screen? You click a button and that's a signature? That doesn't count. They need you to sign something. With a pen." Her mother said "pen" the way other people said "under oath."

Audrey rotated her chair. "I think it counts."

"You think."

"I'll check," Audrey said, which was, in her household, the polite form of "you're wrong," and she turned back to the screen and typed into the search bar: does clicking agree count as a signature. Her mother dried a plate with the slow deliberateness of someone waiting to be proven right.

The results came up in the usual jumble, law firm pages with stock photos of confident people shaking hands, and then a government page, plain and beige, about something called the ESIGN Act. Audrey read it twice. The US ESIGN Act, passed in 2000, said a signature or contract may not be denied legal effect solely because it is in electronic form. She sat back. Her mother had been assuming the opposite, that paper was the real thing and the screen was a toy, and the law had settled the question the other way before Audrey was old enough to have a question. She felt the incipient satisfaction of a person about to win an argument, and also, beneath it, something less comfortable, because if the click was real, then the gray column of text she had scrolled through was real too.

"Mom," she called. "The ESIGN Act. It says a signature can't be denied legal effect just because it's electronic. It's from 2000."

Her mother appeared in the doorway again, towel still on her shoulder. "So it counts."

"It counts."

"Huh." Her mother absorbed this with visible effort, the way she absorbed the fact that the car could parallel park itself. "So when you clicked accept on all those apps."

"I was twelve. Different problem."

Her mother went back to the dishes, and Audrey turned to the screen and did not click the button. That was the part her mother hadn't asked about and Audrey hadn't volunteered: the reading of it. Before, clicking "I Agree" had been a reflex, like blinking. Now she understood it as a signature, and a signature, her father liked to say, was an epigram you wrote with your name, a small compressed promise. His actual line was "a signature is the shortest essay you'll ever write," which Audrey had found embarrassing at eleven and accurate at seventeen. The arbitration clause bothered her. It said disputes would be resolved individually, not in court, and though she could not have explained the whole machinery of it, she understood that she was agreeing to give something up, silently, in advance.

She opened her email and wrote to the store's manager, a woman named Petra whose replies came in a bright green font. Audrey asked, in the most unhurried language she could manage, whether the arbitration provision was standard or negotiable, and whether she could be sent the terms as a document she could look at properly instead of scrolling through in a window designed, she suspected, to catalyze exactly the kind of skimming she had nearly done. She reread the email four times, deleted the word "superfluous," and sent it.

Petra answered within the hour, green font and all: totally fine, most people don't ask, here's a PDF, and also, if it helps, you can come in Saturday and sign the paper version, we keep copies in the back. Audrey printed the PDF, all nine pages, and spread them on the kitchen table, and her mother paused over them on her way with the laundry. "See," her mother said, tapping the signature line at the end. "Paper. Now it's real."

"It was already real, Mom. 2000."

Her mother frowned at the pages, then at Audrey, and seemed about to retreat, but instead she pulled out the chair across from her and sat down, which she almost never did in the middle of a chore. "What's all this then, if it was already real."

Audrey slid the arbitration section across the table. "That's the part I'm not sure about."

Her mother read it, lips moving slightly, a woman who signed things for a living, payroll forms and permission slips and the mortgage, and who had never once been asked what any of it meant. She looked up. "You're going in Saturday anyway?"

"To sign the paper one, yeah. Petra offered."

Her mother tapped the page once more, gently now, like patting something alive. "Take a pen from the drawer," she said. "The good one."

story:
Antoine arrived at the Gateway Cinema twenty minutes early, which he understood immediately to be a mistake, because it left him nothing to do but stand under the marquee rehearsing the opening line he'd already planned: something about how he'd never actually seen Jaws on a big screen. The showing had been Priya's suggestion, sent in a text he had read eleven times, and he had agreed with a speed he later regretted, since eagerness, his older sister insisted, was legible from across a room. He bought the tickets anyway, both of them, an act that felt munificent in the moment and miserly in retrospect, depending on which of his two competing theories of dating he let win.

The first theory he'd absorbed from his cousin Marcus, who held that a first date was a performance to be survived, every silence a deduction, every stumble a permanent record. The second theory he'd gotten from a podcast he'd half-listened to while mowing the lawn in June, something about a psychologist, Erica Boothby, who'd published a study in 2018 on what happened after people talked for the first time. The host had said the finding out loud and then laughed about it, and Antoine had laughed too, alone with the mower, and then forgotten it until this exact moment, standing under the marquee with two tickets going damp in his hand.

Priya arrived at four minutes past seven, waving from across the parking lot in a way that erased, temporarily, both theories. "I'm so sorry, my mom needed me to carry the recycling bins, and then she needed to tell me a whole story about the recycling bins," she said. "Did you already get tickets? You didn't have to do that."

"It was nothing," he said, which was casuistry of the most ordinary kind, since it had been something, and he had wanted it to be something, and he handed one over before she could reach for her wallet.

They found seats in the middle of the tenth row, and the pre-movie silence between them was not the silence he had feared. She asked whether he'd seen it before; he deployed his opening line about the big screen; she said she'd seen it exactly once, at her grandmother's house, with commercials, and that her grandmother had talked through the entire shark. "Like the shark could hear her," Priya said. "Like she was negotiating with it." Antoine laughed harder than the joke strictly required, and she looked pleased, or he thought she looked pleased, and there was the trouble, right there, the whole machinery of guessing.

The movie itself did the work for a while. He let himself watch her more than the screen, in glances he tried to make untraceable: how she leaned forward during the opening night swim, how she whispered "oh no" at the puppy on the beach, how she clutched the armrest during the Orca's descent and then, without ceremony, let her hand drift the last two inches until it rested beside his. He moved his own hand toward it the way you approach a horse. She did not withdraw. Their smallest fingers overlapped for the last forty minutes of the film, and neither of them said anything about it, and neither of them moved, and Antoine understood that this was the subtext doing what subtext does, carrying a conversation neither of them would risk out loud.

It was afterward, in the parking lot under the sodium lights, that the first theory staged its counterattack. She'd checked her phone twice during the credits. She'd said "that was so fun" in a tone he now replayed as obligatory. She'd hugged him quickly, a hug with air in it. Marcus's voice returned with a full inventory: the joke he'd fumbled about the mayor, the moment he'd talked too long about his community college schedule, the terrible stretch where he'd explained the ending of another movie she hadn't seen. Walking home along Center Street, he assembled the case against himself with a prosecutor's care, and by the time he reached the bridge over the creek he had almost convicted them both, himself for his performance and her for having to sit through it.

Then the podcast surfaced, whole this time, the way forgotten things do. A 2018 study by Erica Boothby and her colleagues. After a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company. He stopped on the bridge and pulled out his phone and searched for it, because he no longer trusted his memory of a June afternoon, and there it was, the finding exactly as the host had said it, and it beguiled him, honestly, the idea that the ledger in his head might be wrong in one consistent direction, that everyone walking home from everyone else's first date was doing this same arithmetic and getting the same pessimistic answer. Not a guarantee about Priya. A tendency about people. He let the two theories stand side by side on the bridge and found, for once, that he didn't have to pick.

He typed and deleted three drafts of a text. The fourth was only: "hand was cold, that's my excuse, what's yours." He put the phone in his pocket and walked the last three blocks without checking it, which cost him something, and then stood in his driveway in the dark, where the phone buzzed once against his leg. He looked at the lit kitchen window, then down at his pocket, then at the window again, his thumb already moving.

story:
Alex arrived at his aunt's apartment with the latkes still warm in a towel-lined basket, and the smell of fried onion followed him up the last half flight of stairs. It was the fourth night of Hanukkah, and the whole family had squeezed into the living room where the good furniture usually sat under plastic. His grandmother had brought her brass menorah, the old one with the dented base, and his cousin Marta had set it on the windowsill facing the street, the way their grandfather used to insist.

He had been asked to light the candles this year, which was new. Usually that was Uncle David's job, performed with a gravity that Alex had always found faintly comic and secretly envied. But David was stuck in Chicago because of the storm, and when his grandmother handed Alex the box of candles, she said only, "You know the order, yes?" He said yes, though standing in front of the menorah he found he did not entirely.

He knew about the shamash, at least. He remembered being small and asking why there was always one candle left alone, higher than the others, and his father saying, "That one's the shamash, the helper," in the voice he used for things that were simply true. What Alex could not remember was which end to start from. He counted the branches with his eyes, four on one side of the helper and four on the other, and felt the room behind him waiting, his little cousins cross-legged on the rug, his aunt wiping her hands on her apron.

He put in a candle on the wrong side first, he realized a moment too late, because Marta, watching from the couch, made a small sound like a kettle deciding whether to whistle. "Right to left," she said, not unkindly, "and you take them out left to right." He moved the candle, and nobody laughed, which somehow was worse than laughter, and then better. He placed the fourth candle where it belonged, then the shamash in its raised seat, and struck the match with a hand that was steadier than he expected.

The menorah's brass had been burnished recently; someone had clearly spent an hour on it, and the flames doubled themselves in the polished metal so that nine became eighteen, the eight and the helper both. His grandmother said the blessings, her voice catching on the second one the way it always caught, and Alex answered where he remembered the Hebrew and hummed where he didn't. His aunt turned off the overhead light and the room rearranged itself around the small fire, faces gone golden, the window reflecting a second menorah back at them from the dark glass.

Afterward there was food, the epicurean chaos his family specialized in: latkes with applesauce and sour cream, the argument about which was correct, the tray of sufganiyot his uncle's girlfriend had brought from a bakery in Queens that everyone agreed was too sweet and everyone finished. Alex sat on the floor with his youngest cousin, who was six and wanted to know why they didn't just light all the candles the first night and be done. Alex started to say something about remembering, about a story he half knew, and stopped, because the six-year-old was already eating a candle's worth of wax off the tablecloth.

Later, at the window, his grandmother found him looking at the candles, which had burned down to uneven heights. "You counted from the wrong side," she said. "Your grandfather did that our first year married. He was an engineer, you know, and he said the directions were arbitrary anyway." She laughed at the memory, or at the idea of arbitrariness surviving forty years of marriage, and Alex laughed too. He told her that he'd been thinking, during the blessings, about how strange it was that the helper candle had to be part of the menorah, that the lighting needed one extra light it wasn't even counting.

"Everything that lights something else gets used up," his grandmother said. "That's not strange, that's Tuesday." She patted his shoulder and went back to the kitchen, where his aunt was already pouring coffee nobody wanted, and Alex stood a moment longer with his forehead near the cold glass. He was still not sure what he believed about any of it, the story or the miracle or the reason his family kept doing this in a country where they could have stopped; but he knew he had lit the candles correctly on the fourth night, after being wrong first, and that some consonance between the two, the wrong and the right, was maybe the whole tradition. He heard Marta behind him, saying his name, asking if he wanted the last latke before his uncle found it.

"Split it with me," Alex said, and turned from the window.

story:
Jordyn arrived at the community garden at eight with a biology textbook, a spiral notebook, and forty dollars of her mother's money for a plot fee. The plot was hers on one condition: she had to run the Saturday morning table where neighborhood kids could ask questions about the science wall, a poster the garden committee had put up next to the tomato beds. The committee chair, Ms. Okafor, had read the poster aloud at the last meeting, stumbling over the words transcription and translation, and had looked straight at Jordyn when she said the senior member usually handles it.

The problem was that Jordyn did not fully understand the poster. She could recite the steps for her exam, DNA to RNA to protein, but on Wednesday her study partner Dev had asked her why the process worked that way, and she had opened her mouth and produced nothing. She got a 74 on the quiz. Her mother said a 74 was fine; the committee said the table started Saturday. So Jordyn brought the textbook to the garden and spread it on the bench beside the basil, determined to build the explanation from the ground up before ten o'clock, when the kids came.

At nine-forty a man in a wheelbarrow shirt, one of the volunteer composters, stopped at the poster and read it frowning. "Copied DNA," he said. "So when a cell copies its DNA, the new molecule is all new material. Like a photocopy."

Standing beside him, a teenager from the apartment on Cypress, maybe thirteen, shook his head. "My brother says it's half old. He says one strand is the original and the other one is new." The two of them looked at Jordyn, because she was the one at the table with the book.

"All new," the man said. "A copy is a copy."

"Half old," the boy said. "He showed me a picture."

Jordyn's first instinct was to say she didn't know and refer them to the poster, but the poster didn't cover it. She turned to the diagram in her textbook, the wide double ladder with the rungs split down the middle, and worked outward from what she could see. If the two strands separated, each old strand could serve as a pattern for a new partner. She traced the arrows with her pen. The daughter molecule on the left held one dark strand and one light one. The daughter on the right held the same. She looked up and said, "It's semiconservative."

"What's that mean," the man said, not unkindly.

She kept her eyes on the diagram so she would not lose the thread. "Each new double helix keeps one strand from the original molecule and pairs it with one newly built strand. So you're both right. It's not all new and it's not all old. Half of each."

The boy leaned over the bench. "Okay, but then what's the poster about? The transcription thing."

That was the part she had faked on Wednesday. She had been treating the whole process as a heuristic, a shortcut, a chant to get through the quiz: DNA to RNA to protein, three words, no meaning. The chant had carried her to a 74 and then failed her in front of Dev, and standing here with two people waiting, she understood that she needed the other way of thinking, the slow one, the one where you look at the picture until the picture tells you something. The garden had taught her that already, in a different register. You could memorize a seed packet, or you could watch a bean split open in the soil over six days, which her plot neighbor Ruth had made her do in June.

So she walked it through on the bench like a garden row. The old strand stays; a working copy gets made off it, and that copying is what the poster calls transcription. The copy goes out, and translation reads it, three letters at a time, and builds a chain of amino acids, which folds into a protein. The man said, "Like a recipe copied out of the safe and taken to the kitchen." Jordyn said that was closer than anything her teacher had said all spring. The boy copied the words semiconservative and transcription into his phone.

Then came the twist. The boy turned the textbook around and pointed at the top of the page, at the diagram number. "This is from chapter sixteen," he said. "My brother's book has the same picture but the labels are different. Why does yours say the old strand is the dark one and his says the light one?" Jordyn looked and found he was right in a way that mattered and didn't matter: the colors were arbitrary, chosen by the artist, while the relationship, one strand old, one strand new, was the fixed thing underneath. She said so, and heard herself say it, and understood that this was the difference between memorizing colors and understanding structure, between the chant and the picture. Whether she could hold onto that way of thinking next Tuesday, in a silent exam room, with no man in a wheelbarrow shirt to explain things to, she genuinely did not know.

At noon she watered the tomatoes and thought about her plot, how every seed she had planted had come from last year's plants, which had come from the year before, a line running back unbroken, and yet nothing in the bed was the same plant. Nothing was entirely new either. The soil had been turned and the stakes repositioned; the whole bed had shifted since June in small, tectonic ways she noticed only in the before-and-after photographs she took each week. Whether the mind worked like that, keeping one strand and building the other, she couldn't prove, and she wasn't going to pretend she could.

Ms. Okafor came by at one with the sign-up sheet for next month's table. "You'll do it again?" she asked. Jordyn was still holding the pen she'd used to trace the diagram. "Let me check something first," she said, and turned the textbook back to chapter sixteen.

Lucas had claimed the kitchen the way his mother claimed a sale rack, decisively and with both arms, and now the counter at his grandmother's house looked like the aftermath of a small pastry tornado. He was making dinner for the whole family, his th announcement of departure for college having prompted, somewhere in the organizational machinery of the household, the idea of a send-off meal cooked by the departing person himself. Breaded chicken, a green salad, and, because he had read three articles about it at two in the morning, homemade mayonnaise. His grandmother, Nonna Rosa, sat at the table shelling peas and narrating his technique in a tone she usually reserved for weather.

"You are adding the oil like it owes you money," she observed. "Slow. Slow, like a scandal developing."

"I'm going slow."

"That is not slow. That is a skirmish."

He was, in fairness, going slowly enough. He had learned the method from a video in which a calm man with excellent forearms whisked oil into a yolk drop by drop, and the mixture had thickened, glossy and obliging, for nearly a minute. Lucas felt the particular pride of a person doing something his phone had promised was possible. Then, somewhere between confident and cocky, he added a glug rather than a drip, and the bowl curdled into something shameful: a oily lake with a sad yellow puddle in the middle, exactly the substance the video had warned him about and exactly the substance he had made.

"It broke," he said. "It split. It's ruined."

Nonna Rosa set down her peas and came over with the unhurried authority of a woman who had survived worse in bowls. She peered in. "Hm. The oil went on strike."

"Do I start over?"

"You never start over. Starting over is for people with no history." She took a fresh egg from the carton, cracked it, separated the yolk into a clean bowl with one hand, a gesture so casual it was almost rude. "Whisk the new yolk. Now, slowly, you put the broken one in, spoon by spoon." She tapped the bowl. "The lecithin and the proteins in the yolk, those are emulsifiers. They hold the little oil drops in the water so it doesn't separate."

"That's it? That's the whole trick?"

"That is the whole trick of many things," she said, which Lucas felt was either profound or an evasion, and possibly both.

He whisked the new yolk pale, then added the curdled mess a spoonful at a time, and it was, he had to admit, a little bit magical: the ruined lake folded in and became sauce again, thicker even than before, holding together with what he could only describe as commitment. In chemistry class last spring, Mr. Okonkwo had covered solutions and suspensions and had once, in a digression about carbon, called graphite and diamond allotropes of the same element, which had bothered Lucas for a week: same thing, utterly different arrangement, utterly different result. This felt like the reverse. Different things, whisked into one arrangement, behaving as a single substance. He mentioned this to his grandmother, who considered it while eating a pea raw.

"So the diamond is the good mayonnaise," she said.

"Basically."

"And the graphite?"

"The broken one. Still carbon. Still egg and oil."

"You think too much," she said, but she said it warmly, the way you'd tell someone they wore too much cologne, and she stole a fingertip of the sauce to taste. She nodded once, which from her was equivalent to applause.

The rest of it came together, more or less. The chicken burned on one edge and was fine everywhere else; the salad required no chemistry beyond ambition. When the family sat down, his uncle asked where the jar of mayonnaise was, and Lucas, with tremendous dignity, indicated the bowl. There was the tasting, the pause, the verdict. His little cousin declared it "yellow and perfect," his father said it was better than the store kind, and Lucas suspected both statements of diplomacy but chose not to investigate, since some suspensions, once questioned, fall apart.

Later, alone in the kitchen with the washing up, he held the last spoonful of sauce over the sink and watched it cling, refusing to drip, an evanescent little structure that would be gone by tomorrow and that he had, twice now, brought into existence. He turned off the tap and called into the dining room, "Nonna, can I take the whisk to college?"

"Take the whisk," she called back. "Leave the bowl. The bowl stays with me."

The form was called Optional Application Paperwork 43-B, and nothing about it was optional. Aaron had been filling it out in the lobby of the county transit office for twenty minutes, hunched over a clipboard with a pen chained to it, and he still could not tell whether section six wanted his mother's address or his emergency contact's.

"You look like you're doing your taxes," said the woman at the front desk.

"Line twelve says to list any employers within the preceding period, but it doesn't say what the period is." He held the clipboard up. "Is it a year? Five years? Since I was born?"

She squinted at it. "People usually just guess."

He didn't want to guess. He wanted the junior records clerk job, the one that paid enough to cover a semester of textbooks, and he suspected that a form processed by the county went into a file that outlasted guesses. He copied his mother's address into line twelve, added his emergency contact in the margin, and made a small note: unclear which is wanted. Then a man in a gray tie opened the door to the back offices and said, "Aaron? I'm Mr. Okafor. Come on back."

The interview room had a whiteboard with the word STRUCTURE underlined twice, left over from some earlier meeting. Mr. Okafor sat down without erasing it. "So. Why do you want to work in records?"

Aaron had prepared an answer that made the job sound important, but the sentence felt like it was trying to aggrandize both the filing cabinets and himself, so he dropped it. "I'm good at making messy things findable," he said. "I ran the equipment spreadsheet for my lacrosse team. Nobody could find anything before that."

"You said on the phone you had a question about our application paperwork."

"I did. The form's hard to follow. Line twelve, especially." He slid the clipboard across the desk and pointed to his note in the margin. "I didn't want to hide that I wasn't sure, so I flagged it instead of guessing. If that's wrong, tell me and I'll fix it."

Mr. Okafor read the margin, then read it again. "You know there's a law about this."

"There's a law about line twelve?"

"A law about the whole form. The Plain Writing Act. Signed by Obama, October thirteenth, 2010." He tapped the clipboard. "It requires federal agencies to write documents for the public in clear, plain language."

Aaron sat with that for a second. "But this is the county, not federal."

"There it is," Mr. Okafor said, almost smiling. "That's the argument I've been having with the compliance office for a month. They say we follow it anyway, as a standard. I say some of our forms predate the idea entirely."

"So line twelve is obsolescent."

"I'd say so."

Aaron looked at the whiteboard, at STRUCTURE underlined twice, and then back at the clipboard. "I don't think you should keep the form just because it's what people know. But I also don't think you should throw it out mid-hiring season, because everyone who applied this month already fought through it. Maybe a revision, with the period defined in line twelve, effective for the next cycle." He stopped. "That's a compromise. I'm not certain it's the right one. The people stuck on this form today are still stuck."

"You disagree with me and with the compliance office in the same breath."

"I disagree with both a little," Aaron said. "Is that allowed?"

"It's the job, mostly." Mr. Okafor took the clipboard back and uncapped his own pen. He crossed out line twelve and wrote beside it, in small neat print, List employers from the last three years. Then he initialed it, like a signature on a small treaty. "The county form will get rewritten when someone with standing complains. Consider yourself someone with standing, if you get the job."

"Which depends on the interview."

"Which depends on the interview," Mr. Okafor agreed. He stood, and Aaron stood, and they shook hands across the desk. On the way out, Aaron passed the front desk again, where the woman was helping a girl about his age with the same clipboard, the same pen on its chain.

"Line twelve," Aaron said, "three years. He fixed it just now."

The girl looked up. "Seriously?"

"Check his initials."

From behind the half-open door to the back offices, Mr. Okafor called out, "That's not how I'd have written the announcement, but it's plain."
