story:
The library smelled like the photocopier's warm toner, and Avery had claimed the corner table by the window an hour ago, spreading out her materials for the debate on Thursday: three articles, a printed transcript, and a logic worksheet she'd been avoiding. The worksheet was for Mr. Okafor's class, due tomorrow, and it was the reason she kept losing her place in the articles. Problem four read: If the bill passes, then turnout falls. The bill passes. Therefore, turnout falls. Below it, a smaller instruction asked whether the argument was valid, and why, and Avery had written "yes?" with a question mark she now regretted, because it looked like she didn't care.

She did care, actually. That was the problem. The debate topic was voter identification laws, and her side had to argue that the laws disenfranchise voters, particularly young voters, particularly voters like her who would turn eighteen in an election year without a driver's license. She had statistics. She had a quotation from a county clerk. What she didn't have was any way to answer Marcus, her opponent, who had a way of talking that made everything sound settled before you'd opened your mouth.

He arrived at four, as they'd agreed, carrying nothing but a phone and a cup of coffee he clearly knew wasn't allowed. "You want to run rebuttals," he said, sitting down across from her, "or you want to run your opening?"

"Rebuttals. You go first. Tell me your best one." She clicked her pen twice, a habit she'd picked up from her mother and hated in both of them.

Marcus leaned back. "Fine. If a law protects the integrity of elections, then it's worth some inconvenience. My law protects election integrity. Therefore, it's worth some inconvenience. That's not even an argument you can touch. It's just logic."

Avery looked at him, then down at her worksheet, and felt something shift, small and mechanical, like a gear finding its tooth. "Say that again," she said. "Slowly."

"I said it's just logic."

"No, the shape of it. If this, then that. This. So that." She turned the worksheet so he could see it. "We just did this exact thing in logic. Mr. Okafor calls it modus ponens." She watched Marcus read the page upside down, his mouth tightening the way it did when he suspected he was being managed.

"And?"

"And it's valid no matter what the parts are. That's the part that's bugging me." She pulled a fresh sheet toward her and wrote it out. If the bill passes, then turnout falls. The bill passes. Therefore, turnout falls. Then, because a strange impulse told her to, she crossed out the words and wrote others above them. If the pigeon glows, then the doorknob sings. The pigeon glows. Therefore, the doorknob sings. She slid the paper across. "Is that one valid?"

Marcus read it twice. "That's nonsense."

"I know it's nonsense. Is it valid?"

"That's a gratuitous question, Avery." But he was frowning at it now, actually looking, and she waited him out. Somewhere behind them, a shelving cart squeaked its way toward the biographies, that same two-note complaint it made every afternoon, a leitmotif she'd been hearing since freshman year without ever once thinking about why the wheel hadn't been fixed.

"Okay," Marcus said finally. "Fine. If the pigeon glows, the doorknob sings. The pigeon glows. So the doorknob sings. Given the if, yes. I guess it's valid." He tapped the page. "Which means your voter thing is valid too. And so is mine."

"That's what I thought at first." She took the sheet back and drew a hard line under Marcus's version: If a law protects election integrity, then it's worth some inconvenience. "But look at your first part. Does your law actually protect election integrity? Valid isn't the same as true. My nonsense one was valid and nothing in it was true. The pigeons aren't glowing, Marcus."

He sat with that for a moment, and she could see him trying to find the trap, the rhetorical move that would put her back on the defensive. "So you're saying my argument's bad."

"I'm saying it's only as good as the piece you haven't shown me. If you bring me proof the law protects integrity, then your conclusion follows. If you don't, it doesn't. I can't do anything about the if. Nobody can. That's the deal." She heard herself and winced internally, because it sounded like a lecture, and because she wasn't sure she was right. There was something she was circling and couldn't land: the possibility that both their arguments were valid and they'd still walk out of Thursday night with one winner, that validity was a small clean room inside a large messy building.

Marcus pulled the coffee cup toward himself, remembered the rules, and pushed it away again. "So Thursday I come at you with the conditional, and you come at me with whether the conditional's true."

"Unless you've got a study that says fraud drops when these laws pass. Then I'm in trouble."

"I've got a study that says eighteen people in one county were turned away and it turned out they were all registered fine." He shrugged. "It's not nothing."

"It's not nothing," she agreed, and copied the nonsense sentence into her notebook, pigeon and doorknob and all, as if it were evidence. It occurred to her that she still didn't know how to weigh eighteen people in one county against a whole state's convenience, and that Marcus probably didn't either, and that on Thursday they would both stand up in front of their classmates and speak with more certainty than either of them had earned.

He gathered his phone and the forbidden cup. "Same time Wednesday?"

"Same time Wednesday. Bring the study." She watched him go, then looked back down at the worksheet and erased her question mark, writing yes in its place, then adding underneath, in smaller letters, valid anyway. Behind her the cart squeaked past again, both notes, the same complaint as always. Avery packed her articles into her bag, left the logic worksheet on top so it would be the first thing she saw in the morning, and carried the pigeon sentence home with her.

The community kitchen on Delancey opened at four, and Rachel had the keys because Mrs. Okafor trusted her, or perhaps because nobody else wanted Thursday nights. Either way she was there alone for the first hour, browning chicken thighs for her mother and brothers, who would arrive at six straight from the hospital where her grandmother was being kept for observation. No one had said the word serious yet. Her mother had said, on the phone that morning, "Just make something warm, Rachel. People need to eat."

She set the dessert for last because it was the part she could control. Caramel sauce, poured over the oranges she'd bought with her own money, because her grandmother hated cake and loved anything bitter-sweetened. She'd read the recipe three times on the bus. Sugar and a little water, then heat, then watch. Her phone buzzed on the steel counter while she weighed the sugar.

It was a message from her father, who had moved out in March and communicated now in careful, formal texts, as though drafting letters to a foreign embassy. "I heard about Abuela. I can be there Friday if you want, or Saturday, or not at all. Whatever your mother prefers. I don't want to make anything harder." Rachel read it twice, put the phone face down, and turned it over again. She typed, "She's still in observation. It might be nothing," and then, after a pause that felt like a decision, "Come Friday." Send. The word observation sat there in her mind, meaning both everything and nothing, the way hospitals used language to hold a door open in both directions.

She poured the sugar into the pan and turned the flame to medium. The recipe said not to stir, only to swirl, and it said the sugar would darken fast at the end, which sounded like a warning dressed as a tip. Her youngest brother, Danny, arrived early with his backpack still on, sniffing at the chicken. "Is that going to be ice cream topping?" he asked, and she said it was for the oranges. He leaned against the counter with the canny patience of a twelve-year-old who knew dessert appeared eventually if you hovered long enough.

The sugar melted and went clear, then faintly straw-colored, and Rachel realized she didn't actually know what she was waiting for. There was no instruction that said now. She searched on her phone with syrup-slick fingers, and there it was, plain as a bus schedule: table sugar begins to caramelize at about 170 degrees Celsius. Below that it was just hot syrup; above it, the sugar browned on its own, no proteins involved, nothing but the sugar changing itself. "It's called caramelization," she told Danny, because he had asked what she was staring at, "the sugar browning by itself, without any proteins. Around 170 Celsius is when it starts."

What struck her, stirring nothing, watching the pale gold deepen by degrees, was that the sugar needed the heat to become itself and the heat could also ruin it. Pull it off early and you had sweet water; leave it seconds too long and it went black and bitter past rescuing. Her mother had said something like that once about her marriage, back when she still explained things, back when Rachel still thought of her as a pedagogue rather than a person improvising. Rachel had rolled her eyes at the comparison then. She didn't now, exactly, though she was suspicious of herself for making it, the way people got sentimental over pans.

She stood at the stove and tried to recalibrate, not the temperature but the evening. Her mother would walk in tired and pretending not to be. Her grandmother might love the oranges or might not be home to eat them. Her father would arrive Friday into a kitchen already full, and Rachel could not know whether that was a repair or a rupture; the heat was on and the sugar was turning and every second changed it. She decided, in the only way available to her, which was by acting. The caramel went amber, then the color of dark honey, and she lifted the pan off the flame.

"Get the oranges," she said, and Danny scrambled for the bowl while she poured, a thin amber rope hissing faintly against the cold peel, hardening as it fell.

Maelle set her laptop on the table between two cold cups of coffee and opened the assignment sheet for the fourth time that afternoon. Write a research paper of eight to ten pages with an argument, footnotes, and a bibliography in a standard citation style. She had written plenty of essays before, the kind where you said what you felt and stopped, but this one demanded that she prove things, and she did not yet know how proof was supposed to look on a page.

Across the table, Dani was highlighting a biology chapter with a green pen she kept borrowing from Maelle's pencil case without asking. Dani wanted to finish by five so she could get to the pool before the lap lanes filled up, and she said so every twenty minutes. When Maelle read the assignment aloud, hoping for sympathy, Dani snorted. "Footnotes? Who decided that? Some committee trying to ruin your life in like 2015, probably."

Maelle typed the words notes and bibliography into the library's search bar. The first result was a scanned page from a thick orange book, its type small and formal, and beneath the scan a line of publication history she read twice. "The Chicago Manual of Style, whose notes-and-bibliography system uses footnotes, was first published by the University of Chicago Press in 1906." She checked the date, then checked it again against the copyright page of the newer edition the library held in its reference section, the physical copy she had carried to the café in her bag.

"Dani. This thing is older than your great-grandparents." She turned the screen so Dani could see. "It's called the Chicago Manual of Style, and the edition that uses footnotes came out in 1906. There were cars, barely. There was no such thing as a teenager, probably."

"That is deeply weird," Dani said, and went back to her chloroplasts.

Maelle had expected rules to feel like fences. What she found instead, working through the sample notes on page 67, was more like a system of debts. Every quotation owed a number; every number owed a page at the bottom; every page at the bottom owed a place in the bibliography at the end. She began drafting an argument about school segregation in her own city, and the footnotes kept interrupting her, which at first she resented and then, gradually, did not. The interruptions made her check herself. When she wrote that a 1974 court order had ended the busing dispute, the footnote forced her to admit, in small type at the bottom of the page, that two of her sources disagreed about what the order had actually required. On the page she could not pretend the disagreement away.

She tried to cajole Dani into reading her third paragraph, promising to buy the next round of coffee, but Dani had her suit in a gym bag under the table and only said, "If it has the word 'furthermore' in it, no." So Maelle read it to herself, mouthing the words. Her thesis had started as a blunt claim, that the city's schools had been deliberately divided, and it had softened into something she liked less and trusted more: that the record showed intent in some districts and only negligence in others, and that the evidence did not let her say which was which in every case. A lemma in one of the law articles she had found, a small preliminary point the author proved before getting to the larger argument, had shown her that a claim could be built in stages, each one resting on the last, and she had begun to structure her paper the same way, proving the small things first.

By six, Dani had packed up and left, and the window of the café had gone dark so that Maelle could see the room reflected behind her document. She read her bibliography through, fourteen entries, every one of them a book or article she had actually opened, and she noticed that none of her sources was about the sectarian fears that had driven some of the opposition, because she had avoided those sources, and she wrote a note to herself to find two of them tomorrow before the draft was due. She saved the file, closed the laptop, and slid the thick orange manual back into her bag, where its weight made the strap sag. The barista began stacking chairs near the door, and Maelle raised her hand for one last cup to go.

Leah sat on the hood of her mother's Corolla with her cap on her knees and the speech on her phone, deleting the sentence she had just written. The parking lot behind the gymnasium had been striped for four hundred cars and held eleven, including Mr. Okafor's van with the magnetic chess decals and a truck she suspected belonged to Deshawn's uncle, who honked every time anyone in a gown walked past.

"You've read it eleven times," said Priya, leaning against the fender with two plastic cups of lemonade balanced on a stack of programs. "Is it eleven times good or eleven times bad?"

"It's corny," Leah said. "Every version is corny. I keep writing stuff like, and as we go forward, let us remember the halls that shaped us, and then I want to lie down in traffic."

"Then don't write that."

"Thank you, Priya. Solved. Let's get nachos."

But she couldn't joke her way out of it, because in ninety minutes she had to stand at a podium and say something to three hundred people who already knew everything about her, and there was no version of goodbye that didn't sound like a greeting card that had been through a laminator. She had tried the taxonomy of commencement speeches in her notebook: the metaphor speech, the anecdote speech, the quote-a-dead-president speech. Every category ended in the same place, the place where sincerity curdled into syrup.

Deshawn came around the corner of the gym with his gown unzipped over a T-shirt that said ASK ME ABOUT MY PLAGIARISM ALLEGATION, which had been cleared in October but which he refused to retire. He read over her shoulder for exactly four seconds.

"Mine's forty seconds long," he said. "Sit down, stand up, thank the cafeteria ladies, get out. Everyone's thinking about the parking lot anyway."

"Forty seconds is its own kind of corny. Contrarian corny."

"Everything is corny, Leah. Graduation is corny by nature. It's a ceremony. Ceremonies are institutionalized corn." He stole her lemonade. "What's the word they keep calling you, by the way? In the program?"

"Valedictorian."

"You know what that actually means? Vale dicere. Latin. It means to say farewell. That's the whole job. That's why the valedictorian gives the speech. You're the farewell person."

Leah looked at him to check whether he was inventing this to mess with her, which was a reasonable default, but he was gesturing at the program with such confidence that she looked it up on Priya's phone, and there it was, plain as a grocery list. The title of the honor she had spent four years earning was not, at root, about being first. It was about saying goodbye. She had internalized a ranking; the word itself had internalized a leaving.

"So the speech isn't an add-on," she said slowly. "It's the meaning of the title. If I skip the farewell, I'm not really the valedictorian, I'm just the highest GPA wearing a special cord."

"Correct," said Deshawn. "Also you've been sitting on the car that long that the hood ornament is hot, so."

Here was the problem, though, and she turned it over while Priya argued with Deshawn about whether the cafeteria ladies deserved thanks (they did; Deshawn claimed his forty seconds already covered it). The farewell was exactly what felt corny, and it was also exactly what the job required, and she couldn't dismiss the corniness as a failure of her own talent. Maybe the feeling itself was honest. Maybe everyone standing in a parking lot in polyester gowns genuinely did not want to say goodbye, and the awkwardness of the words was just the awkwardness of the thing, undressed. The judicious move was not to find cleverer words but to let the words be a little stupid on purpose, the way people say I love you at airports.

She typed. "Priya. Priya. Listen. 'Four years ago I would have told you valedictorian meant the person with the best grades. It doesn't. It comes from the Latin vale dicere, to say farewell. So I'm not up here because I'm the smartest. I'm up here because someone has to say it, and they gave the job to me. Here's the thing: I don't want to. None of us want to. That's the entire situation.'"

Priya put her cup down on the roof of the Corolla. "Say the middle part again."

"'None of us want to.'"

"Okay, that's not corny. That's just true."

"It's going to sound corny," Leah said, "and I've decided that's fine. Corny is the tax on meaning it. I'll pay it."

"You'll pay it," Deshawn agreed solemnly, and then the side door of the gym banged open and a woman with a clipboard leaned out and shouted that the valedictorian needed to come inside now, right now, they were lining up.

Leah slid off the hood, folded her cap under her arm, and jogged toward the door, and she was three steps into the gymnasium, squinting in the fluorescent light, before she realized she had left her phone on the hood of the car with the only copy of the speech still open on it.

Through the propped door she could see Priya holding it up, waggling it at her like a prize on a game show, and Deshawn already narrating to an uncle she'd never met: "Forty seconds, ladies. That's all anybody needs."

story:
The office of Henry's mentor smelled of coffee and old paper, and on the desk between them sat two hearing aids in an open case, small and pinkish, like something borrowed from a doll. Mr. Voss had been a live sound engineer for twenty years before he started mentoring students through the arts program at Henry's school, and he had never once mentioned the hearing aids until today, when he took them out to clean them in the middle of their conversation about Henry's college audition tape.

"You can keep talking," Mr. Voss said, working a tiny brush along one of them. "I'll catch up."

Henry had come here with a real problem, and the problem was not the audition tape. It was that Dex had texted him last night, after their fourth concert in two months, and the text was still sitting on Henry's phone like a stone in his pocket. He hadn't answered it yet. Instead he watched Mr. Voss's hands move with the ease of a man who had done this ten thousand times, in bathrooms and vans and backstage corridors, and he thought about how a person ends up carrying a small case everywhere he goes for the rest of his life.

"Play me the second track again," Mr. Voss said, fitting the aids back behind his ears. "The one with the turgid strings. You told me it was supposed to feel heavy, but to me it just feels muddy." He turned the laptop toward Henry. Henry pressed play. The strings swelled, thick and slow, filling the small office, and Mr. Voss closed his eyes and conducted a little with two fingers, and Henry almost forgot the phone in his hand.

Almost. He unlocked the screen instead, and read the message again while the music ran. "Saw the audiologist today. She says long or repeated exposure to sounds at or above 85 decibels can cause hearing loss, and the damaged hair cells in your inner ear do not grow back. Mine's probably fine, mild, but she asked how loud my shows are. Man, we stand right at the front. Every time." Dex had ended it with, "Are you getting the ringing too? Beseech you, tell me you're not getting the ringing."

"What's that you're reading?" Mr. Voss asked, not accusing, just curious, the way he asked everything.

"A friend." Henry set the phone face down on the desk, then turned it over again. "We go to shows. A lot of shows. He went to get his ears checked because of the ringing, and he sent me this thing the doctor told him." He read it out loud, the decibels, the hair cells, the part about them never growing back, and watched Mr. Voss's face do something complicated and brief, like a window shade caught by a gust.

"Yeah," Mr. Voss said. He didn't launch into anything. He just tapped his ear, once, lightly, the way you'd touch a bruise to see if it still hurt. "That's how it goes."

"You never said."

"You never asked." He leaned back. "Besides, what would I have said? Don't do the thing that made you love music in the first place? That's a turgid speech if I ever heard one." He smiled at his own word, and Henry laughed, and then neither of them laughed, because the office was quiet and the audition tape had ended and the hearing aids were doing whatever hearing aids do in the silence.

Henry told him about the ringing. He told him about the show in March where they'd stood against the barrier for three hours and he'd heard a thin whine for two days afterward, how he'd noticed it in the shower, how he'd noticed it again last week in the library when the room was empty and it was still there, faint, like a wire somewhere under the floor. Mr. Voss listened with his whole body, which was his way, and then he opened a drawer and set a pair of foam earplugs on the desk, still in the wrapper, the kind you buy at a pharmacy for two dollars.

"Take them or don't," he said. "That part's yours."

Here was what Henry turned over on the bus home, window open, wrapper in his fist. Part of him wanted to believe the ringing was nothing, the way a person wants to believe a stain will wash out; Dex's audiologist had said his own damage was mild, probably, and Henry's was probably milder still, and there was a whole loud future out there, parties and basement shows and the front row, and earplugs felt like arriving at a funeral. But another part of him kept looking at the small pinkish case on the desk, and the two fingers conducting, and thinking about how Mr. Voss had never gotten to choose, back then, because nobody had told him, and now he carried the consequences in a case that clicked shut. Henry had been told. That was the difference. That was the whole difference, and it sat on his chest like a hand.

He didn't know everything, and he tried to be honest with himself about that. He didn't know whether his ears were already damaged, or how much, or whether the whine in the library was permanent or would fade the way the one after March had mostly faded. He didn't know if he would even keep the plugs in his jacket pocket or lose them in a week. But he knew what Dex's message said, and he knew what Mr. Voss's face had done, and he could hold both of those at once, the fun and the future, without pretending either one away. That was all discernment was, he decided, not wisdom exactly, just refusing to drop one of the things you were carrying.

At his stop he texted Dex back with one hand while the doors hissed open. "Getting it too. Library, quiet rooms, sometimes. Keep the plugs they gave you?" Then, after a minute, standing on the curb with the bus pulling away: "Next show, I'll be the guy in the back with orange foam in his ears. Meet me there." He put the wrapper in his pocket, where he could feel it, and walked home.

story:
Mackenzie found her father in the kitchen, holding a red plastic cup he wasn't drinking from, and she knew before he said anything that he wanted to talk about the money.

The party had spilled from the living room onto the porch and the brown lawn beyond it, half the senior class milling around under string lights her mother had hung that afternoon. Someone had made a playlist that everyone complained about and nobody changed. Mackenzie had spent the first hour being hugged by people she would never see again, and each hug had felt like a small withdrawal from an account she hadn't realized was finite.

"So State sent the final package," her father said. He set the cup down on the counter beside the bowl of pretzels. "It's doable. With the loans, it's doable."

She had known this was coming. She had rehearsed for it in the shower that morning, which now struck her as ridiculous, rehearsing for a conversation with her own father. "And Amherst?"

"Amherst is Amherst." He rubbed the back of his neck. "They gave us more aid, actually. More than I expected. But there's still a gap, and the gap has your name on it for ten years."

"Nine years," she said. "The loans are nine-year terms. I looked it up."

Her father laughed, short and surprised, and for a second the kitchen was almost easy. Then he said, "Your grandmother would tell you to go. She'd say people like us don't turn down places like that." He paused. "People like her, I mean. She never got to finish."

That was the lever he always used, though he used it gently. Mackenzie's grandmother had left college in 1968 after two semesters, and the family had been narrating that departure ever since, turning one woman's decision into a parable that could be deployed for any purpose. Go because she couldn't. Or be careful because she taught us what debt does to a family. The story contextualized whatever you wanted it to.

"I need to think," Mackenzie said, and she took a cup of her own, filled it with punch she didn't want, and went out to the porch.

Dex was sitting on the railing with his gown still on, unzipped, the sleeves rolled to his elbows. He'd worn it all evening like a dare. "There she is," he said. "Salutatorian. Second-best in the county."

"Second in the school, not the county."

"I'm contextualizing." He slid over to make room. "So what did he say?"

She told him, mostly, leaving out the grandmother part because that part was hers. "He wants me to say it's fine either way. He says it's my choice. But he says it in the voice he uses when something costs too much at a restaurant."

"Ah, the plutocracy problem," Dex said. "Rich kids don't even fill out the forms. The rest of us get to decide which kind of hostage we'd like to be."

"That's very pithy."

"I've been workshopping it." He kicked his heels against the railing. Across the lawn, Priya Nair was attempting to teach Dev Okonkwo to salsa, and failing, and both of them were laughing so hard the lesson had become something else entirely. Mackenzie watched them and felt the grief arrive on schedule, the one everyone had warned her about, the strange mourning of an ending that hadn't technically happened yet. Tomorrow she would hand in her laptop and her parking pass, and the building would go on without her, and by August the halls would smell like a different cohort's mistakes.

"I keep thinking it's over," she said. "That's all I've thought about for weeks. That it's ending. Tonight everyone keeps saying congratulations like it's a finish line."

Dex looked at her for a moment, then drained his cup. "You know what the ceremony's actually called? Commencement. That's the word. It means beginning. They started using it for graduations because the graduates commence a new status. Like becoming a bachelor or a master. It's a beginning thing, not an ending thing. It's literally in the name."

"Where did you learn that?"

"Mr. Ferraro told our class in April and I've been saving it for exactly this moment." He spread his hands, presenting the fact like a magician producing a card. "You're welcome."

Mackenzie turned the word over. She had walked across a stage that morning in a cap that kept sliding, and she had been sad, and everyone had been sad, and apparently they had all been sad at a ceremony named for starting. There was something almost funny about it. There was also something in it she couldn't dismiss, though she tried, because Dex had a habit of finding one true thing and wielding it like it settled everything.

"That doesn't actually decide anything," she said. "About the money."

"I know. It's just a word."

"It's not just a word, though." She set her untouched punch on the railing. "If it's a beginning, then the debt is part of the beginning. It's not the price of something I'm finishing. It's the terms of something I'm starting." She heard how it sounded, like a decision, and she hadn't made one. "Or that's just a nice way to talk myself into nine years of payments. I can't tell yet."

Dex nudged her shoulder with his. "You'll figure it out. You're the salutatorian."

"Second-best," she said.

Inside, her father had come to the screen door with his empty cup, watching the lawn, and she thought about going in and telling him she'd decided, and she thought about going in and telling him she needed one more week, and she thought about how her grandmother, whoever she was becoming in the family's retelling, must once have stood in some kitchen weighing one life against another with no ceremony at all to name it.

Priya had given up on the salsa and was pulling people toward the grass for a group photo. "Mackenzie!" she shouted. "Dex! Get in, you can't miss this."

Mackenzie jumped down from the railing and took Dex's hand to pull him with her, her fingers still tacky from the punch, and stood in the back row where the tall people went, squinting into the flash.

story:
Maelle spread the two articles across the library table like cards she'd been dealt, though she hadn't chosen either of them. The first was a dense Danish study following more than half a million children, its tables stretching across pages like frost on a window. The second was older, shorter, a 1998 paper in The Lancet. Her assignment sheet, folded twice in her pocket, said compare and evaluate. It did not say how to begin when two sources disagreed so completely that one of them had to be wrong.

She had claimed the table by the periodicals at four o'clock, when the afternoon light came through the tall windows and warmed the varnished wood. Now it was past six, and the light had gone the color of weak tea. Her pen had produced three sentences, all of which she had crossed out. A boy two tables over was sleeping with his cheek against a sociology textbook, and somewhere behind the reference desk a printer chunked and sighed, chunked and sighed.

The problem, she decided, was that she kept trying to decide which article won. She read the Danish paper's numbers again, then flipped to the older one, and this time she noticed something she had skimmed past before. The 1998 paper, the one claiming a link between the MMR vaccine and autism, had been based on only twelve children. She sat back. Twelve. The other study had followed over half a million, and this one, twelve. She counted the word children with her finger on the page as though the number might change if she touched it.

"What are you grinning at?" said Priya, dropping into the opposite chair with a granola bar and no apology. Priya worked the circulation desk on Thursdays and had made it her policy to investigate anyone who looked either delighted or devastated near closing time.

"Twelve," Maelle said. "This whole paper, the one that scared everybody about the MMR vaccine and autism, it was twelve kids. That's smaller than my homeroom." She turned the page toward Priya, who squinted at the dense type and shrugged.

"That's it? That's your discovery?"

"It's not just small. It's that nobody told me the size until today. I read about this in middle school like it was a fact, like it was the same kind of thing as gravity." She tapped the Danish paper. "And then this one, half a million kids, saying the opposite. So my review isn't really about vaccines at all. It's about how you decide who to believe."

Priya unwrapped her granola bar and considered this with the seriousness of someone being paid ten dollars an hour to shelve returns. "So say that. Isn't that what a critical review is?"

Maelle didn't answer right away, because the honest answer was that she had been hoping a critical review was a thing with rules, a formula she could accede to the way she'd acceded to the five-paragraph essay all through high school, and what she was actually looking at was judgment. The vernacular of her English classes, thesis and evidence and clincher, suddenly felt like a dialect from a country she'd left. She tried to say some of this out loud and it came out clumsy, and Priya said, "So write it clumsy and fix it after."

By seven thirty the library had thinned to the sleeping boy, a man at a computer watching something with the sound off, and the two of them. Maelle had filled four pages in her looping handwriting. She had written that the Danish study's strength was its scale, that the Lancet paper's weakness was hers to name and she named it plainly, and then she had written a paragraph she was less sure of, about how a small study could still raise questions worth asking, even while it couldn't answer them. She wasn't certain that paragraph was right. She underlined it in pencil, which was her private mark for things that might be wrong.

"There's a thing I can't figure out," she said as Priya began stacking chairs. "Whether finding the flaws counts as being critical, or whether it's just being jaundiced. Like, when does careful stop and bitter start?"

Priya set a chair on a table, upside down, and thought about it for exactly as long as it took to pick up the next chair. "Maybe that's the part you write honestly," she said. "That you don't know."

Maelle looked down at her underlined paragraph, then at the two articles still lying open beside each other, the enormous study and the small one, both printed on the same ordinary paper under the same fluorescent hum. She picked up her pen, turned to a fresh page, and wrote the first sentence of her last paragraph: What remains uncertain to me is.

story:
The U-Haul was still in the driveway when Aidan started walking, because if he stayed to unpack one more box he was going to call Dezi and say something he'd regret. Dezi had wanted him to fight for it, had gone pugnacious on the last night, saying things like "make them un-move you" as though the decision had been his to lose. Aidan walked instead, past strip malls still under construction, until the air conditioning of the public library hit him like weather.

He found a table near the periodicals, second from the window, and spread his phone and a paperback across it like a man claiming territory. He did this the next afternoon too, and the one after that, nodding at the librarian who had started saying "back again" in a tone he couldn't classify as mocking or kind.

On Thursday a girl with a lanyard full of enamel pins sat down across from him without asking. She opened a battered notebook and wrote what looked like an essay, occasionally glancing at him as though he were furniture she was still deciding about.

"You're new," she said finally. "I'm Priya. I do my reading here because my house has four younger siblings and zero quiet."

"I'm between houses," Aidan said, which was technically true and sounded less pathetic than "I don't know anyone."

Priya came back the next day, and the day after, and gradually their exchanges lengthened from weather to teachers to whether the town's only good burrito place was a myth. When she learned he'd arrived from a city three hours south, she asked what he missed, and he said "everything" and then, embarrassed by the size of it, "this coffee place where we all hung out. It sounds stupid."

"It doesn't," she said. She flipped her notebook to a page she'd apparently prepared, which he found both alarming and endearing. "There's this thing we studied in sociology. Sociologist Ray Oldenburg, in his 1989 book The Great Good Place, called them 'third places'. Cafes, libraries. Where people meet outside home and work."

Aidan turned that over for a second, his thumb marking his page. "So home is first and work is second."

"School counts," she said. "The point is the in-between."

He had been thinking of the move as a subtraction, friends and haunts lifted out and nothing put back. The idea that the space between home and school was a thing with a structure, a thing a person could walk into on purpose, rearranged something in him. He'd assumed he would acclimate by endurance, gritting through the semester until the town stopped feeling foreign. Maybe instead you could build it, deliberately, one repeated table at a time.

That weekend he tested the theory. He tried a diner where the waitress refilled his coffee without asking, and a game store where the clerk talked to him for ten minutes about a tactical RPG, and both were fine and neither was it. On Monday he was back at the library table by four, and when Priya arrived he'd pushed his paperback to one side to make room, an act so small he almost didn't register doing it.

"Verdict?" she asked.

"Pending," he said. "The diner had good pie but no Priya." She rolled her eyes, but she was smiling at her notebook, and he understood that he had given something away.

Still, he was honest enough with himself to know the theory had holes. His old coffee place hadn't worked because of architecture; it had worked because Dezi had dragged him there the first week of ninth grade and because Marcus's sister worked the counter and let them linger past close. Oldenburg, whoever he was, couldn't have scripted that. Third places might be found or built, but the people inside them arrived by accident or by the slow accumulation of afternoons, and Aidan couldn't control that part. He only knew that sitting at the same table had raised the odds, and that raising the odds was all he had.

In October, Dezi texted a photo of the coffee place, the old corner booth, Marcus's hand giving a thumbs-up. Aidan looked at it for a long time, feeling the pull of what he'd lost and the strange counterweight of what he was assembling here, unable to say which one was supposed to win. Then he screenshotted it, set his phone down on the library table, and turned it toward Priya.

"That's them," he said. "The original third place."

story:
The grill had been his mother's territory, and for three months after the funeral nobody had touched it, so that the cover had gone stiff with rain and the propane tank sat in the corner of the yard like a mourner who refused to leave. Eli dragged the cover off on a Saturday in June because his aunt and cousins were coming at six, and because someone had to make dinner, and because his father, who could talk for an hour about deconstructing a Bowie album, went silent whenever a kitchen timer beeped.

He'd found the recipe in his mother's handwriting, a marinated chicken breast with lime and cumin, folded twice and slipped into a cookbook as if she'd meant to come back to it. He'd never grilled anything in his life. He'd watched her, though, the way you watch a parent doing something ordinary, which is to say barely at all, and so his memory was mostly of her wrist turning the tongs and the smell of smoke in her hair when she came inside.

The coals were uneven, one side blazing and the other sulking, and the chicken sizzled when he laid it down at an angle she might have chosen. He turned it after four minutes and saw the pale underside, the meat still slack and translucent at the edges. His cousin Delia, fifteen and merciless, had already asked twice whether they were going to eat before dark.

He cut into the thickest breast with a paring knife. The juices ran faintly pink, or maybe it was the marinade, and he crouched over the plate on the picnic table trying to decide, and deciding, in his experience, never actually settled anything. It was like the college essay he'd been drafting for two weeks, the one about whether honesty obligated him to tell admissions that his junior-year grades had collapsed the semester his mother was sick, or whether grief was a reason that could extenuate without excusing. He'd written four openings and deleted three.

His father came out with a beer he wasn't drinking and stood at his shoulder. "Don't guess," he said, and held out a thin metal wand with a wire, a digital thermometer from the drawer by the stove, still in its plastic sleeve. "Read the box."

Eli slit the sleeve with the paring knife. The card inside, in small print, said US food safety agencies say chicken is safely cooked when its internal temperature reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer. He read it twice, then held it up so his father could see he'd read it. "A hundred and sixty-five," he said.

"Then find out what you've got."

He pushed the probe into the thickest part of the breast, avoiding what he guessed was bone, and the display climbed through the nineties, the low hundreds, and stalled at 152. He'd nearly talked himself into pulling the meat off when the number ticked up again, 158, 161, and he stood there watching digits the way his mother used to stand watching the door for his father to come home from a gig that ran late. It reached 165 and the display blinked, and he moved the probe to a second breast and found 168 already, and to a thinner one that read 151, and he learned in those few minutes that a grill was not one temperature but a dozen arguing ones.

While the smaller piece cooked he thought about a kid from his debate team, Marcus, who had organized a food drive the same spring Eli had stopped answering texts, and who had called him once in April, not to recruit him, just to ask if he was eating. Eli had said yes, which was true on technicality, cereal and the leftovers his aunt left in foil. Marcus hadn't asked again. Eli had admired him for that, and resented him slightly, too, because there was something about a person whose altruistic instincts ran so clean that it made your own flinching look like a character flaw. He suspected Marcus of being genuinely good, and he suspected that some people would call that naive, and he could not fully decide which suspicion was the slander.

Dinner, when it finally happened, was fine. Delia ate two breasts and said nothing, which from Delia was a review. His father ate slowly and said, "This is hers. The lime thing." Not a question. Eli said yes, and didn't add that he'd doubled the cumin because he couldn't remember whether she doubled it or he was inventing a version of her that never existed. Some frauds were deliberate; he was beginning to understand that others were just memory doing its best work with bad materials, a charlatan who believed his own pitch.

Afterward, alone in the blue dark with the tongs and the foil and the plate of bones, he turned the essay over in his mind again. Maybe he would write it plainly, the semester and the reason, and let the admissions reader decide what weight the reason carried, the way the thermometer had let the chicken decide whether it was done. Or maybe he'd close the grill, go inside, and open a new document, blank and cool, the cursor blinking at him from the corner of the screen.

story:
The apartment was thirty minutes from campus by bus, third floor, with a balcony just wide enough for one chair, and Dev had sent the lease to all three of them that afternoon with a single line: "Read it tonight, we sign tomorrow." William opened the file at his desk, the fan pushing warm air across the back of his neck, and began at the beginning, because that was the kind of person he had decided to be this year. The first pages were dull in a way that felt almost physical: recitals, definitions, a section titled "Terms and Conditions" that ran to eleven paragraphs. His eyes wanted to slide. He made them stay.

It was in section fourteen that he stopped. The clause said that the tenants would be liable, jointly and severally, for all rent and damages under the lease. He read it twice, then pasted it into a search bar. The results came back fast and flat and changed the shape of the evening: under joint and several liability, each of several people who share an obligation can be held responsible for the entire amount, not only their own share. He sat back. He and Dev and Priya were each planning to cover a third of the rent. The landlord, apparently, did not care about thirds.

He called Dev first, and Dev laughed before William had finished the sentence. "So if Priya bails, we cover her part. Obviously. That's what friends do."

"That's not what it says," William said. "It says if Priya bails, either of us can be made to cover all of it. Not her third. All of it. The whole rent, every month, until the lease ends."

There was a pause long enough that William could hear a television in the background of Dev's room. "That can't be right," Dev said. "That's ridiculous."

"It's right. I'm reading it right now."

Priya joined the call a minute later, breathless from somewhere outdoors, and William walked them through it again, slower this time. He had spent the last hour with the document, sequestered at his desk with his phone face down, and he had worked out the arithmetic more than once, hoping it would come out differently. It did not. If one of them lost a job, the other two were not exposed to a share; they were exposed to everything.

"So we don't sign," Dev said.

"We want the apartment," Priya said. "It's two blocks from the river. It's the only one we can afford, and affording it is exactly the problem, so."

William turned in his chair and looked at the printout he had made, six pages of it, clause fourteen circled in pencil. His father had signed things his whole life, he thought, shift contracts, a truck loan, papers he never read, and called that practicality. William had always privately considered it a lack of acumen, an older man's carelessness dressed up as toughness. Now he was less sure which of them was being naive, the man who signed without reading or the boy who imagined that reading was the same as control.

"We could do a side agreement," he said. "Between the three of us. If the landlord makes one of us pay more than a third, the others owe that person the difference. It doesn't change what we owe the landlord, but it changes what we owe each other."

"That sounds tautological," Priya said. "We'd be signing a contract to enforce the contract we already agreed to by being friends."

"It's not the same thing," William said, though he could hear the weakness in it. "One of them is legally enforceable and one of them is us trusting each other, and after tonight I'd rather have both."

They argued for another twenty minutes. Dev wanted to sign the lease as it stood and trust the friendship; Priya wanted to ask the landlord to strike the clause entirely, which William doubted would work and Priya suspected he only doubted because he liked knowing things. In the end they agreed to the side agreement, drafted in a shared document while they were still on the call, three signatures to be scanned by noon.

William drafted it himself, and it was almost midnight when he noticed the message waiting below the thread. It was from Priya, sent an hour earlier, before they had agreed on anything. She had written to the landlord asking about removing clause fourteen, and the landlord had already replied: the lease had been generated for three tenants, but joint and several liability was standard, and if they preferred, it could be rewritten for a single tenant with two occupants, which some renters found simpler. A single tenant. One name, one obligation, no shares at all.

William read the reply three times, then called her, and she picked up on the second ring.

"You already sent this," he said. "Before we decided anything."

"I sent it before I knew what we'd decide," Priya said. "I wanted to know what our options were." In the quiet that followed, he could hear her walking, her footsteps on pavement somewhere between the river and home. "My parents would co-sign for me alone," she said. "They offered. I didn't tell you because I wanted us to figure it out together, and now we have, and I still don't know if I'd be helping you both or just making sure I'm the one who's safe."

William looked at the side agreement open on his screen, his own name typed into the first signature line, and found he could not tell either.

"So what do we do?" Dev's voice came from the other line, where he had apparently been listening the whole time.

William reached for his pencil and turned back to clause fourteen, the circle he had drawn around it already smudged gray. "Tomorrow," he said, "we go in together, all three of us, and we don't sign anything until every line has been read out loud."

story:
Mr. Draper's laptop cart had seventeen working machines and twenty-six students, so Lucas spent the first ten minutes of GIS class watching Devin play solitaire. When a Chromebook finally came free, it was the one with the space bar that stuck, which meant every command arrived twice. Lucas typed "flood" and the program asked him, politely, twice, whether he meant flood.

The assignment was to overlay two layers of the city map, flood risk and housing density, and write a paragraph about what the overlap meant. Mr. Draper had said the word "overlay" the way some people say "lasagna," like it was the whole meal. Lucas pulled the flood layer first, and the river appeared as a blue tongue licking through the middle of town, wide at the south end where the old warehouses were. Then he added housing, and the dense blocks, orange and red, clustered along the tongue like they were trying to get close to it.

"That's the point," said Priya, leaning over from the next desk. "People live where the water wants to be."

"The water wanted it first," Lucas said. "We just moved in anyway."

He knew the south side a little. His grandmother had lived there until the spring the creek came up through the floor vents, and after that she'd moved in with his grandfather on the north side, in the house with the filing cabinets in the basement. That was where Lucas had been on Saturday, looking for a badminton set, when he found the cabinets instead.

They were full of maps. Not printed maps, though some of those too, but sheets of tracing paper, dozens of them, each one drawn in colored pencil and labeled in his grandfather's small upright hand. Soil. Water table. Slope. Woodland. One sheet was nothing but the floodplain, hatched in blue, and under it another showed the same city with houses inked on like scattered seeds. Some sheets were stacked and pinned together at the corners, and when Lucas held a stack up to the basement's single bulb, the layers went translucent and the whole city showed through at once, water and houses arguing in the same light.

His grandfather came down for a shoebox of tax papers and found Lucas holding the stack against the bulb like a slide.

"Careful with those," he said. "Those took a summer."

"What are they?"

"Landscape architect named Ian McHarg had the idea, back around sixty-nine. His book was called Design with Nature. You stacked your maps, soil, water, all the factors, and the stack told you what the land could take." He took the pinned sheets gently out of Lucas's hand and laid them flat. "We did it by hand. It took weeks."

Lucas had looked at him, then, with the strange feeling of a door opening in a wall he'd thought was solid. "We're doing that," he said. "In class. On computers. Except it takes about four seconds."

His grandfather had smiled at the ceiling. "Everything you can do in four seconds, somebody spent a summer on first."

Now, in class, Lucas added the third layer, the one Mr. Draper hadn't asked for, a soil map he found in the public data folder, and the south side went dark where the floodplain and the housing and the soft ground all agreed. The software called what he was doing a layer stack, and the phrase felt borrowed, like something that had been sequestered in a basement for fifty years and let out.

Priya was still watching his screen. "What's the extra layer?"

"Soil. My grandfather drew this exact map by hand. Tracing paper. Colored pencil." He dragged the layers apart and together again, watching the overlap bloom and shrink. "Same idea. He got it from a book."

"He invented GIS?"

"No. The book just had the idea, the stacking. The computers came after and automated it." Lucas zoomed in on the littoral streets near the river, the blocks that touched the water like a shoreline, where the orange of the housing sat squarely on the blue of the flood risk. "That's where my grandma used to live."

The paragraph Mr. Draper wanted was supposed to say what the overlap meant, and Lucas found that the harder he looked, the less single it became. The maps said the houses shouldn't be there, but the maps also couldn't say that Ms. Arroyo had run her shop on Delancey for thirty years, or that the soft soil was the reason the rents were low enough for people to stay at all. Priya's position was clean: move people out of the floodplain, build on the high ground. His grandfather's was its counterpoint: the land decides, and you listen to it before you draw a single lot. Lucas suspected the truth needed both of them and maybe a third one he hadn't found yet, and he wrote that, honestly, at the bottom of the paragraph, in the space where a conclusion was supposed to go.

He printed the map, color being the whole point, and that evening rode his bike across town to the north side. His grandfather was in the basement again, shoebox open, receipts spread like fallen leaves. Lucas held out the printout: the blue tongue, the orange blocks, the dark argument where they met.

"Same map," his grandfather said.

"Not quite," said Lucas. "Yours is prettier."

His grandfather put down a receipt and reached for his reading glasses. "Show me where the creek comes up through the floor," he said.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
story:
John had taken the warehouse job for one summer, to save money for a laptop before junior year, and by the second week he understood the arithmetic of the place. Eleven dollars an hour, no overtime unless the manager approved it, and shifts that ran until midnight whenever a truck came in late. His hands had hardened around the box cutter; his shoulders had learned the particular ache of lifting from the knees anyway, because his supervisor, Mrs. Okoye, kept correcting him until it was inculcated, the way she said it, until lifting the right way was as automatic as breathing.

The trouble started on a Thursday, when the ammonia-based cleaner in aisle nine made Ramon sick. Ramon was fifty-three, worked two jobs, and had been at the warehouse longer than the warehouse had been a warehouse. He sat on an upturned crate in the break room, gray-faced, waving off anyone who tried to help. "It's the fumes," he said. "They switched suppliers. That stuff is noxious, and they don't dilute it, and when I asked for gloves they said budget." John got him water from the cooler and sat down across from him, and that was where the conversation began, though John didn't know it yet.

"We should do something," said Priya, who worked the scanner station and was saving for nursing school. "Complain. All of us, together."

"We can't," said Marcus, a lanky kid who'd just started, like John. "They'll just fire everybody. That's how it works. My uncle tried something like this at his plant and they cut his hours till he quit."

"They can't just do that," Priya said. "There's a law. The big one. My mom's in a union at the hospital." She frowned, trying to pull the name out of the air, and failed, and Marcus rolled his eyes, and the conversation began to dissolve into who knew whose uncle and what had happened to whom.

That night John looked it up. He'd meant to check his pay stub against the hours he'd written in his phone, but the break room argument kept circling in his head, and so he typed the words instead: are workers allowed to organize. He found it faster than he expected. The National Labor Relations Act, signed on July 5, 1935, gave most private-sector workers the right to form unions and bargain collectively. He read the sentence three times. Most, not all. Private-sector. He didn't understand everything it implied, but he understood the shape of it: there was a legal floor under what Priya wanted to do, and Marcus's uncle's story, whatever was true in it, wasn't the whole truth.

He printed the page at the library in the morning and brought it to the break room folded into quarters. "The National Labor Relations Act," he said, when everyone was there, even Ramon, who had come back despite the headache. "Nineteen thirty-five. July fifth. It gave most private-sector workers the right to form unions and bargain collectively." He set the paper on the table between the microwave and the vending machine. "So we're allowed. I think we're allowed."

Marcus picked it up and read it himself, lips moving slightly. "Most," he said finally. "What's the 'most' mean? What if we're not in the 'most'?"

"I don't know," John said. It cost him something to say it, in front of everyone, but he said it anyway. "I don't know what happens after, either. Whether it's a vote, or how long it takes, or whether they find some other reason to let people go. I just know the starting part is legal."

What happened next was smaller than anyone expected and larger than John had imagined. Mrs. Okoye, who had come in for her coffee and heard all of it from the doorway, said nothing about unions. She took the printed page, read it, handed it back, and said only, "Ramon, go home sick, officially, on the record. Priya, write up what the cleaner did and have everyone who saw it sign." Then she went to the office, and by the next afternoon there were gloves in the supply cage, diluted solution in the yellow bottles, and a laminated sign about ventilation that nobody read but everybody noticed. Ramon's daughter came to pick him up that day, and Priya walked out to the car with her, holding the signed write-up in a folder like it was something that mattered.

Marcus stayed late on Friday, unloading a truck beside John, and between the last two pallets he said, "I'm still not sure about the union part. I think maybe we fix things one at a time and that's enough." John stacked his boxes and thought about it, both things at once, the law that made them a "we" and the gloves that had arrived without it. "Maybe," he said. "But if they switch the cleaner again, I want us to already know we can do more." Marcus considered this, wiped his hands on his jeans, and said, "Then keep the page." John folded it back into quarters and put it in his pocket.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
story:
Samantha had put off learning to drive for two years, which her mother attributed to sensible caution and her grandmother attributed to cowardice, and which Samantha herself, on the morning of her first lesson, could not explain in fewer words than either of those. The driving school occupied a strip unit between a nail salon and a tax office, its waiting room furnished with a plastic ficus and a wall of framed certificates. She signed in at seven minutes to nine, holding her permit the way she held a hand of cards she didn't trust herself to play.

The instructor was a small man named Mr. Okafor who had taught in Lagos, then Toronto, then here, and who mentioned all three cities in the first five minutes as if establishing his credentials as someone no road could surprise. He led her out to a white sedan with a brake pedal on the passenger side, and he had her adjust the mirrors, and he had her set her hands at ten and two, and then he sat back and folded his arms and looked at her.

"You want to drive out of this lot," he said. "Fine. Start the car."

She turned the key. The engine caught. She checked the mirror, put her hand on the shifter, and Mr. Okafor did not move.

"Something's missing," he said.

She looked at the mirrors again. She checked the dash for warnings. Then she followed his gaze to the belt lying slack against the seat beside her, and the heat came up her neck so fast she nearly apologized out loud for her whole existence. She pulled it across her body and clicked it in.

"Thank you," Mr. Okafor said. "Now we drive." He said it without the lecture she had braced for, and she appreciated that, though she also noticed that the absence of the lecture left the silence doing the work of one.

Her mother was a trauma nurse who had spent sixteen years inculcating in Samantha a particular relationship to automobiles: not fear exactly, but a kind of liturgical respect, seat belts invoked the way other families said grace. Her father, who had left when Samantha was eleven and sent postcards from cities she had to look up, had held the opposite faith. He believed the belt was a leash, that statistics were for people who didn't know how a car felt underneath them, that a good driver made his own luck. Samantha had spent her childhood being driven by both of them, holding the door handle in her mother's car and leaning her head against the window in her father's, and she had never fully decided which of them to believe.

They did three laps of the industrial streets behind the school, and on the third lap Mr. Okafor had her merge onto a boulevard where the speed limit was forty and the traffic moved like it had somewhere better to be. Her hands sweated on the wheel. A delivery truck straddled its lane, and she braked harder than she needed to, and Mr. Okafor's pedal never came down, which she counted as a kind of praise.

At a red light, a woman in the next lane was steering with her knees while she scrolled through her phone, and Samantha watched her in the mirror. "My dad says belts are for people who drive badly," she said, because the silence had gone on long enough that something had to fill it.

Mr. Okafor considered this without taking his eyes off the road. "The CDC says wearing a seat belt cuts serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half," he said. "Half. And it doesn't say only for bad drivers." Then the light changed and he said, "Go," and the conversation was over.

She drove the rest of the lesson with that number sitting beside her like a passenger. Half. Not all, which was her mother's version, the version that had kept Samantha out of the driver's seat until eighteen. Not nothing, which was her father's. Half was an honest fraction, and she found she liked it less than either extreme, because a number like that made you choose anyway. It didn't tell you whether you were in the half that survived or the half that didn't, and it didn't tell you whether the belt itself was freedom or leash, or whether those were even different things.

Afterward, in the strip mall parking lot, Mr. Okafor filled out her progress sheet. "Control is good," he said. "Confidence will come." He tore off her copy and held it out, and as she took it he added, "Same time next week," in a tone that assumed she would say yes.

Her grandmother was idling at the curb in her enormous Buick, and Samantha got in, and reached, out of habit older than memory, for the seat belt. The buckle hung up halfway down the door pillar, the old fabric gone stiff, and she had to feed it back through with two hands while her grandmother watched with an expression that was not quite disapproval and not quite its opposite.

"Your father never wore his," her grandmother said, pulling out into traffic.

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Natalie had carried the fragments to school in a shoebox lined with a dish towel, and through first period the box sat in her locker like something breathing. In the art room, fourth period, she finally opened it on the counter near the window: seven pieces of her grandmother's rice bowl, the celadon glaze catching the light along edges sharp enough to matter. Mr. Ferreira wandered past, glanced in, and said nothing, which was the reason she had chosen his room and not the ceramics studio, where Ms. Okoye would have asked questions.

The bowl had broken on Tuesday. Her grandmother had been napping, the apartment warm and smelling of barley tea, and Natalie had reached over it for the good brushes her grandmother kept in a jar behind the stove, the ones she never used anymore because her hands shook. The bowl had been under a cloth. That was all. It had not even made much of a sound, just a settling, and Natalie had stood there with her grandmother's brushes and her grandmother's broken bowl, sixty years of a life in pieces on a linoleum floor.

Her first plan had been glue and paint. There was a kit in her backpack, cyanoacrylate and a tiny bottle of green acrylic she had mixed to match the glaze, because her grandmother's eyes were going but not that gone. The plan was simple and it was a lie, and both of those things had recommended it. She had even rehearsed the sentence: I found it like that. She laid the pieces out now in their rough circle, and the jagged lines between them adumbrated a shape she couldn't name, a map of the moment her hand had knocked against cloth.

Priya leaned over from the next table, brush in her teeth, hands black with ink. "Whose is it?"

"My grandmother's. Was." Natalie turned one piece over. "I'm fixing it before Sunday. She's making rice for the equinox thing and she'll want it."

"You're going to fake it." Priya said it without judgment, the way she said everything, and set her brush down. "You could fake it. Nobody would know."

"I would know." Natalie heard how it sounded, like a line from a movie, and hated it, and meant it anyway. She had spent two days weighing the truth against her grandmother's face when she saw the bowl, and the truth kept losing. Her grandmother had come to this country with two suitcases and a sister, had been impecunious for decades in a way Natalie only understood in fragments, stories about washing dishes in a restaurant that served food from home. The bowl was from home. It had crossed an ocean in a rolled sweater. It was the only object in the apartment her grandmother had ever called by a name.

Priya pulled out her phone, typed, scrolled, and turned the screen around. Natalie read it twice. A photograph of a mended bowl, black seams running through it like rivers drawn in ink, and every seam blazing with gold, so that the breaks were the most alive part of the thing, more visible than they would ever have been unbroken.

"Kintsugi," Priya read. "It's a Japanese technique of repairing broken pottery with lacquer mixed or dusted with powdered gold." She looked up. "It treats the break as part of the object's history instead of hiding it."

Natalie took the phone and read further, past the bright photographs, into the practice of it: the lacquer, the curing, the weeks it took. Real gold, real urushi lacquer that could blister her skin, patience measured in months. She thought of her cheap kit, the acrylic paint, the rehearsed sentence, the whole small hegemony of pretending nothing had happened, and she understood that she had been weighing the wrong things. She wasn't choosing between truth and her grandmother's face. She was choosing what the bowl would be for the rest of its life: an object with a scar, or an object with a secret.

"It takes months to cure," she said. "Properly. I have five days." Mr. Ferreira, watering the paint sinks like a man tending a garden, said from across the room, "Some things you can't speed up," and nothing else. Priya was already scrolling again, muttering about mica powder and epoxy and a craft store two bus transfers away, and whether a girl on a babysitting income could afford even the fake gold. Natalie swept the fragments gently back into the towel, folding it over them the way her grandmother folded wrappers, corners first.

At the craft store she stood a long time in front of two options: gold leaf she could not afford and a small jar of mica powder the color of a struck match. She bought the mica. On Sunday she would set the bowl on the table, seams rough and glittering where they should have been lacquered and smooth, and she would not say I found it like that. She would say something else, though she did not yet know what, and she practiced nothing on the bus ride home, only held the shoebox on her lap with both hands and watched the mica gold shine through the cloth every time the doors opened and the light came in.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
story:
Raphael's grandfather had a desktop computer in the room that used to be an office, and that was where Raphael sat on Saturday morning with his project due Monday. The assignment was to overlay a flood risk map and a housing map of the city on one screen and write about what the overlap meant. The teacher had given them a trial version of the software and a folder of files, and Raphael had assumed the hard part would be the writing. It was not.

The housing map loaded first: parcels of land drawn as clean outlined shapes, thousands of them, each one clickable, each one carrying an address and a year built. When he dragged it around, the parcels undulated across the screen in a slow ripple as the software redrew them, thin blue boundaries breathing over the gray background. Then he opened the flood map and something entirely different appeared. It looked like a photograph, like weather radar on the news, a smear of colors from pale yellow to deep red, soft-edged and grainy when he zoomed in until he could see the individual squares of it, one blocky cell at a time.

He tried to put one on top of the other and the software refused. A gray box told him the layers did not match. He clicked through three menus, closed the box, opened it again, and went to find his grandfather, who was sorting seed packets at the kitchen table with the radio murmuring ball scores.

"Can I ask you something about maps?"

His grandfather set down a packet of marigolds. "I drew maps for the county for thirty-one years. Ask."

"On the computer. One of my files looks like shapes, outlines you can click, and the other one looks like pixels. Like a photo. They won't stack."

His grandfather was quiet for a moment, the way he was quiet before he answered anything worth answering. "The pixel one," he said. "That's raster." He turned another seed packet over in his hands. "The shapes are the other kind. Look it up, kiddo. I only ever drew the lines."

Raphael looked it up. It took him twenty minutes of reading and another twenty of squinting at the software's help pages, and then he sat back in the stiff office chair with the strange satisfaction of a door swinging open. The shapes were vector data, built from points, lines and polygons, and that was why each parcel could carry its own record, its own little encapsulation of address and age and owner. The pixel map was raster data, a grid of cells, each cell holding exactly one value, which in this case was a flood risk score. One value per square. That was why zooming in showed him blocks instead of boundaries. The two maps weren't broken; they were two different languages describing the same city.

The problem of stacking them turned out to be a problem of translation. He found a tool that converted his vector parcels into the same grid as the flood map, and watched the tidy polygons dissolve into squares. Something was lost, he could see that immediately. Two narrow lots became one fat cell. A sliver of park disappeared entirely, too thin to claim its own square. He sat with his hand on the mouse, circumspect now in a way he hadn't been an hour ago, because he understood that every choice about how to merge the maps was also a quiet claim about what mattered. If he made the cells smaller, he kept the slivers, but the flood map's cells were the size they were, and he couldn't invent precision that wasn't in the source.

He ran it anyway. The overlay bloomed on the screen, and there it was: a band of red and orange running through the east side where the housing grid was densest, block after block of cells sitting squarely on top of parcels built in the forties and fifties. He printed it on his grandfather's old printer, which groaned like it disagreed, and carried the warm page to the kitchen.

"This is it," he said. "This whole neighborhood. High flood risk, and it's the most crowded part of the map." He laid the page on the table between the marigolds and the tomatoes.

His grandfather put on his glasses and leaned close, tracing the red band with one finger. "Your great-aunt lived right there," he said. "Water came to her porch steps in '77. Twice since." He tapped the dense grid of squares. "You know what I can't tell from this, though?"

"What?"

"Which of those squares is a family that can absorb a flood, and which is a family that can't." He handed the page back. "That's not in anybody's data."

Raphael stood there holding the map. He had a page due Monday, eight hundred words, and now he knew what at least the first paragraph would say: that the grid could tell you where the water went, and the shapes could tell you who lived there, and both of them together still left the most important thing unnamed. He didn't know yet how to write that without it sounding like giving up. He went back to the office, set the printed map beside the keyboard, and opened a blank document. On screen, behind the cursor, the city's parcels still rippled in a slow wave, red squares holding their ground beneath them.
